PROVISION FOB GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY-* INTERIM APPRORPIATION
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide that a sum not exceeding $648,333,333.33 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances for loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending the thirty-first day of March, 1944, for the purposes and subject to the terms, conditions and limitations set out in the resolution presently on the orders of the day, to provide that sums not exceeding $3,890,000,000 be granted to His Majesty, and being one-sixth of the said amount of $3,890,000,000.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Bradette in the chair.

If I understand what is going on, this is a resolution to provide one-sixth of the military expenditures for the year. Who will audit those expenditures? There is an officer of the House of Commons, the auditor general, whose duty it is to check the expenditures of all departments. This officer originally was directly under the control of parliament, not only the House of Commons but also the Senate. What has happened? The duty of compiling the reports has been transferred from the office of the auditor general to the office of the comptroller of the treasury, which means that one of the prerogatives of members of parliament-and I use that expression in the widest sense as meaning members of the Senate and1 of the House of Commons-has been given to the Department of Finance. So that essential part of the work of the auditor general is no longer carried on by his office but by the comptroller of the treasury, an official of the treasury department. With the very best of good-will, we cannot approve of that. It means that some of the rights of parliament are transferred to a department which already is too large.
What has happened? In the first place there was a transfer of 125 employees from the office of the auditor general to the office of the comptroller of the treasury, to compile the reports previously compiled by the auditor general. First an establishment was made.

Then a treasury board minute was passed. There was some shifting of the staff, following which a pool was made of the transferables. An order in council was passed authorizing the transfer. Approximately 125 employees of the office of the auditor general were transferred to the branch of the comptroller of the treasury. The names of those employees appear in the Canada Gazette for the month of March. Following that the auditor general's branch made a request for a hundred new employees. That was done for the purpose of effecting some reclassification, and to give a chance to the pets of the officers in the department to obtain better salaries, under the pretence of improving the public accounting of the country. The real reason was reclassification; they got rid of employees they did not like, having them transferred to the office of the comptroller of the treasury. Then the way was open for the reclassification they desire. It is interesting to note that a man who had been fired from an experimental farm in western Canada twelve years ago, following a report from the office of the auditor general, is now one of the new appointees in that office.
I hold in my hand an ordter in council supplied at my request by the late Mr. Rinfret oh February 8, 1939. This memorandum was prepared by the auditor general on March 24, 1934, when he was comptroller of the treasury. At the time there were many who expressed the view that the memorandum was dictated by Mr. Bennett himself when lie was prime minister, and when in one of his outbursts he decided to remove the, accountants from various departments where they had chances of promotion.
This was done under the advice of the present deputy minister of finance. I do not know the position taken by other hon. members, but I have already expressed the opinion that the present deputy minister of finance should be superannuated. I still hold that view, in spite of the defence the minister has repeatedly made respecting this gentleman. Why? For the reason that he is always trying to do something to bring about more and more centralization, and to have more power. This time he gets part of the power which was under the control of parliament, but which is now under the control of the Department of Finance. Let me tell the committee once more that I know how this is done. It is worked in a very simple way. In the first place, if anything has happened it is due to the laziness and idleness of the auditor general and his officials. It is because.

War Appropriation
as the minister has said, the auditor general is not qualified for the functions of the position he now occupies as chief accountant for this country. He is not a certified accountant, but rather a lawyer who practised for some time in western Canada. He is a man who is interested in gathering historical facts. That is an interesting pursuit for a gentleman of leisure, but not for one occupying the position of chief accountant of a country like ours. That is the very reason, or one of the reasons, given yesterday by the Minister of Finance when explaining the shift of work from the branch of the auditor general to the Department of Finance. It is precisely because of that idleness and laziness that the reports were cut, and that, in the first place, all the items below $5,000 were not put in, and, in the second1 place, all the items below $25,000 were deleted from the auditor general's report.
.Now we find a shift of work. They drop 125 employees and take on a hundred more. Where is the economy? It is just a matter of giving those people an opportunity to give promotion to their pets. That is the way it goes. On the other hand it has satisfied the greed for more power and the desire for synchronization which fills the heart of the deputy minister of finance. On the one hand the lazy have less to do, and on the other the centralizer has more power at his disposal. He has a larger number of employees.
Do you not think, sir, that it is the summit of absurdity to have the audit made by an official of the House of Commons, but that the report of that audit should not be made by him but rather by the comptroller of the treasury? It is compiled by the comptroller. This I cannot understand, and in my opinion it requires an explanation.
Let me tell the minister that if he wishes to improve the situation with respect to the audit he must in the first instance superannuate-and I employ a euphemism-the deputy minister of finance. Secondly, he must repeal the Bank of Canada Act, abolish the Bank of Canada and put Mr. Towers on foot. In the third place he must abolish the foreign exchange control board, and in the fourth place he must abolish the wartime prices and trade board. Then he must restore the powers and duties the Minister of Finance exercised before. All this I believe sincerely the present incumbent is able to fulfil most satisfactorily for the public good. That is my humble view. But this takes courage. It takes courage to undo what Mr. Bennett did, without sufficient reason. It must be undone. When we are
on the wrong road, if we wish to make progress the only thing to do is to retrace our steps on the wrong road until we come to the intersection with the right road, and then proceed along- the right road. That, sir, is my humble view in the. matter.
The minister is entitled to think what he likes about his own deputy minister; he has the right to hold any view he wishes about him, just as I have. I will tell him some more about him. Some people consider it an insult to be called incompetent. A lawyer is usually incompetent as a shoemaker. It should not offend the lawyer to say that he would be incompetent as a shoemaker, no . more than it should offend a shoemaker to tell him he would be incompetent as a lawyer or a doctor. I suggest to the minister that he replace the present doctor of economics who is acting as his deputy by a man who has had sound and practical experience in banking, whether that has been obtained in Canada or in any other country. He should have a man who has considerable experience of life and a knowledge of facts, not a man who is ready to experiment on such a large scale as the whole Dominion of Canada. I shall not say more for the moment.
I should like the minister to give us a clear explanation of what has been done regarding the report of the auditor general.
I should like to know why employees are being taken away from the direct jurisdiction of parliament and transferred to his own department. I have indicated a few reasons why I think this has been done, but I know [DOT] there are others. I am sure the minister will find it rather hard to explain why this report of his own officers is not in the same form as it was in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The reasons for changing
the form of the auditor general's report and the public accounts are set out in a speech which I made on July 31, 1942. If the hon. member will look at the proposals as outlined by me at that time he will find that no final or ultimate responsibility is transferred from the auditor general' to the Department of Finance. I think that answers his principal complaint. The details of the plan of the report will be found at the bottom of the second column of page 5082 of Hansard, where the following appears:
To be more specific, the contents of the single report would be organized substantially as follows:
(a)	Part I, to consist of an over-all survey and report of the financial operations of the year in such form as will clearly portray the policies followed.
(b)	Part II, to consist of the balance sheet of Canada, certified by the auditor general.
War Appropriation

(c)	Part III, to consist of the revenues of the year classified by departments and sources; t iis to be signed by suitable executive officers and certified by the auditor general.
(d)	Part IV, to consist of expenditure statements as submitted by the comptroller of the treasury and certified by the auditor general.
(e)	Part V, to consist of miscellaneous statements as may be necessary to report all transactions not included in the preceding parts.
(f)	Part VI, to consist of the report of the auditor general on the statements in the preceding parts and on such other matters as he is required to report to the House of Commons.
It will be found on examination of that plan that the auditor general does not transfer an3r of his responsibilities to the comptroller of the treasury or to the Department of Finance. With regard to the transfer of officials I may say that the writing or the compiling of the report will be done to a much greater extent by the comptroller of the treasury than heretofore, and to a lesser extent by the auditor general. As I explained last night, there are two documents. One is the public accounts and the other is the auditor general's report. To a considerable extent these are duplications. As I said in July last, the present plan is an improvement. Let me quote what I said on that occasion as follows:
It will, I think, be apparent at once to the bouse that a single report of this type will be an enormous convenience to members in their work of analysing and appraising the multifarious transactions which are necessarily involved in the receiving and spending of a sum of money approximating four billion dollars. When sums of this magnitude are expended in millions of individual transactions, the work of the member who seeks to understand the operations of government is bound to be difficult enough in any case; it is incumbent upon us, I think, to see that he does not have to wade through a chaotic mass of material scattered over two massive volumes, each covering largely the same field but in a different way. It seems to me, also, that presentation of the accounting records relating to expenditures on the same basis as the details in the estimates should facilitate a better control by the house when voting supply.
The hon. gentleman suggests that the scheme was devised for the purpose of enabling certain officials to obtain promotions. That was no part whatever of the purpose of the scheme. I do not know what the results have been in that regard1. The hon. gentleman says that there has been a transfer of 125 officials from the auditor general's department to the comptroller of the treasury, and that 100 officials had been appointed to the auditor general's department. The charge that these transfers have been made for the purpose of effecting promotions is unfounded. That may have been the result in some cases, but certainly this is the first suggestion I have heard that
(Mr. Ilsley.]
that was an integral part of the plan. I think those are the main points raised by the hon. gentleman.
With regard to the discussion of these matters on this motion. I suggest that this resolution and the bill to be founded thereon be permitted to go through. We will then take up item No. 3 on the order paper, which is the resolution preceding the war appropriation bill for this year. I submit that that would be a more appropriate time for a discussion of general matters, some of which have been discussed on this motion for interim supply.
Has the minister anything to say about the observations I made last evening in connection with the meagreness of the report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has complained from time to time about the lack of detail in and the meagreness of the reports. With regard to the new plan, I had this to say on July 31:
In regard to the degree to which itemization of detail will be carried, it will be noted that responsibility for decisions in this field will in effect have to be assumed by the Minister of Finance, because the deputy minister of finance and the comptroller of the treasury are his officials. Probably the Minister of Finance should be in a better position than anyone else to give directions as to the nature of the break-down necessary to elucidate transactions of interest to the house. If the minister does not go far enough to satisfy hon. members he can be called to account on the floor of the house.
In so far as I personally am concerned, my attitude will be to place primary emphasis on the necessity of disclosing to the house all information that is really useful in enabling it to perform its essential functions. Naturally, in regard to war expenditures, considerations of secrecy will have to be kept in mind because of the necessity of not giving aid to the enemy; in regard to all expenditures there are also considerations of man-power shortage and cost which call for every practicable economy consistent with the public interest. In this latter connection I may add that I hope the new procedure will lead to certain savihgs in staff and in cost by the elimination of some duplication existing at present in the accounting work of the Department of Finance and the auditor general's office.
The public accounts and the auditor general's report for the fiscal year 1911-1942 are now in the course of preparation and must be ready this autumn. It is impossible to effect the various changes in organization and staff and the necessary adjustments in accounting systems in time to implement the recommendations I have outlined above, in connection with the reports now in preparation. If, however, the recommendations are satisfactory to the house, they will he put into effect in time to have their results appear in the report for the current fiscal year, which will be issued in the fall of

War Appropriation
1943. I am advised, however, that the auditor general's report for the last fiscal year is being enlarged so that the house will receive a fuller disclosure of information, for which some members have been asking. Last year, for reasons beyond the control of the audit office, it was found to be impracticable to bring together a tabulation of payments to war contractors, charged to the Department of National Defence, at any figure under $25,000. That task, it wrill be noted, is statistical rather than audit, but the audit office has installed a punch-card equipment which will enable the record to be carried down to payments as low' as $10,000, a figure which should give a good over-all coverage. I believe an attempt will be made to make the record as illuminating as possible w'ithin the limits imposed by necessary considerations of secrecy. In regard to the departments generally, there w'ill be certain variations in the details of the accounting record. In some cases a break-down of expenditures under a particular vote into payments of $1,000 or less will be necessary to give a clear picture of what has happened, while in other cases a $5,000 minimum may tell the story fairly. That, I understand, will be the general objective of the auditor general-to tell the story in all cases in as clear and simple a way as may be practicable.

I shall take only a moment because I have no desire to prolong the discussion.
The minister in his statement a moment ago said in reference to the 1942 reports that last fall when the reports were in course of printing, they would perhaps ,be fuller. I cannot see how they could be any less full than they are. Take' the Indian Affairs branch of the Department of Mines and Resources, item 160, appearing at page 171 of the auditor general's report for 1942. Indian agencies are there referred1 to in one line. In the 1939 auditor general's report, the last of the formerly complete reports, eighteen pages are taken to refer to Indian agencies, of which there are 121 in Canada. I always felt it my duty to inquire into the auditor general's report to the greatest extent I could. I could not inquire into everything; that would be impossible, but one of the departments I always liked to inquire into was the Department of Mines and Resources, because it covers far-off areas through which I have travelled extensively. But how much information could I find in one line about Indian agencies in the auditor general's report of 1942? There are, as I have said, 121 Indian agencies. I have travelled on many an Indian reservation and made careful observations to bring matters up in the house. I cannot for the life of me see how this house is to keep track of expenditures unless we have before us some information upon which we can base inquiries. But when there is only one line of information we cannot inquire about anything, can we?
At page 171 of the auditor general's report for 1942 I find this: Indian agencies, appropriation, $654,893, expenditures, $630,435.46. I might want to inquire about an agency in Ontario or in Manitoba or any other province, but there is nothing in the report upon which I can base a question. Let me give the minister an illustration of what I mean. Some few years ago an item went through for approximately $7,000-I am giving it from memory-for a hospital. I asked where the hospital was to be built, and was told it was to be built on such and such an Indian reservation. The following summer, at a great deal of expense to myself, I chartered a boat in northern Ontario and went six miles down a small river to a fair-sized lake. It took me two or three days to get to and from the reservation to see that hospital. When I got there, what did I find? I found a log building, perhaps fifty by fifty, or it might have been fifty by sixty, or forty by seventy-I have forgotten the dimensions, but it was about that size. There was not a window in it, and it was full of hay. I inquired, "Is this the hospital?" It was to be a hospital, they told me, "but now we are using it for a barn." There was an item for several thousand dollars for a hospital that was without a window and was filled with hay.
There was another item, I have forgotten for how much money but it was a considerable amount, for a tractor for an Indian reservation. At great expense to myself, by boat and with Indian guides,. I visited that reservation, and what- did I find? A field of approximately ten acres on which potatoes could, be raised. Fancy a tractor for ploughing up a ten-acre field! There was no more ploughed land than the ten acres. In the following year I had not an opportunity to bring these matters before the house. I shall not name the reservation now, because it is so long ago, but I have all the figures. When the estimates came up for Indian Affairs the house was within an hour or more of prorogation, and when one attempts to bring up a matter so close to the end of the session there is no opportunity for discussion because all one hears is "carried," "carried," "carried." That is what always happens when the estimates come up in the last hour of the session. The Minister of Finance will not approve anything like that, I feel sure. I have the utmost confidence in him if he knows what is going on. Nor am I saying a word against the minister in charge of the Department of Mines and Resources, because he could not possibly have the time to investigate everything in his department. I happened to have
War Appropriation

the time to investigate these items concerning che Indian reservations. I like to: investigate and to present to the house what I find out, not by way of criticism, not by way of faultfinding, not suspecting that there is anything wrong, because I would not say there was; but merely so that I can present to the house reasons for making a change perhaps in what is being done.
That is the only reason I have been complaining in the last couple of years against the meagreness of these reports. I hope the minister will not think I am small in mentioning perhaps these minor items. They do not compare, of course, with the expenditure of millions, but if we watch the pennies the dollars will look after themselves.

I do not wish to prevent the minister from getting his resolution and bill through because I know the Minister of National Defence is waiting to go on with the war appropriation bill. But I do want to point out, Mr. Chairman, that the things which are being done in the name of the war surprise not only members of parliament but the country as well. The government is taking altogether too much from the taxpayers, and it is costing too much to get it. Last night we voted one-sixth of the civil estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1944, and then we have the resolution for $3,890,000,000. You can only raise the money from two sources, one of which is taxation and the other, borrowing. As you know, Mr. Chairman, I rose in this house in 1940 after !he war had started and referred to the dead hand of the treasury as we spent money like water, and the waste and' useless duplication. I called attention that year, again in 1941 and last year, to the powers of the auditor general under section 41 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. At that time it was found that the auditor general did not have jurisdiction to audit war accounts in the appropriation bill although as auditor general lie was and is responsible alone to parliament. He is responsible to parliament for the expenditure of all the moneys. I took up this question of the audit during the estimates of 1940 and 1941 and again last year; and I went into the audit act, defining the powers and functions of the auditor general, responsible as he was to this house done for the accurate and complete examination of the accounts of Canada and the reporting of them to the House of Commons. I was very much astonished in this connection to find out that the auditor general had not the power to veto anything, not even a

single dollar. All he could do was to report to the House of Commons what he thought was out of the way.
When I found that the auditor general's report contained little or nothing by way of a check on these expenditures I called the attention of the house to the fact. Another official known as the comptroller of the treasury was appointed, I believe in 1931, by the former government, and the present auditor general had that position. He was a competent man, Mr. Watson Sellar, I knew him for years. He served a faithful Minister of Finance, the late Mr. Robb, who was mindful of the taxpayers' money. I wrote the auditor general a letter last June, and he told me that he had no power over the war appropriation bill, but the comptroller of the treasury had over the bill we are referring to now, that is, the war expenditures bill of nearly four billion dollars. I learned from the officials, regarding the rise of war expenditures, reflected in the items set out in this resolution and the bill before us, that if the comptroller of the treasury found that any item of this $3,890,000,000 was within the text of clauses (a), (b), (c) or (d) of the resolution on the order paper, namely, the security, defence and peace of Canada, the conduct of her military affairs, the promoting of trade and industry, and the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary for the war, he must simply put his stamp on the account. I wrote the Minister of Finance a letter. The minister made a speech, a copy of which I have, on Fridaj% July 31, the day before the sessional business was practically concluded1-we closed on Saturday, August 1. The minister did make a reply, which is in Hansard of that date, suggesting some changes in our audit methods; I admit that.
While I have a great deal of respect for the government of the day and the war ministers, I am surprised to see what is going on in the name of the war. Some expenditures which are under civilian estimates are duplicated in other spending departments of the army, the navy and the air force. With this high taxation, I fail to see where the taxpayer is getting value for his money. If you vote this one-sixth you may as well pass the whole bill; the money is provided, and the three ministers with the Minister of Finance can do what they like about it and that is the end as far as the House of Commons goes. Once you pass this bill and this resolution you have lost for all time the control of every dollar of that war expenditure. That is the situation the moment

War Appropriation
you put the seal of approval on this particular resolution, which has to be backed up by the bill which is now before the committee of the whole house.
I had a reply from the Minister of Finance on this matter on September 12. True it is that he had a victory loan campaign on and no doubt it was impossible to give an explanation before. But he refused to give a tabulated comparison between current expenditures and what was spent before the war in the same departments, the number of officials, and the cost of them, to this house and to the committee. Probably he did not have it. But I can say that the members of the House of Commons are totally ignorant of what the war is costing from day to day. Although we have three good ministers in charge of the armed forces to explain in detail their departments, it is my opinion that the taxpayers are being charged too much, a lot of it not for war at all; money is costing too much, the war loans are costing too much, and we are not receiving the information we should have.
If all this money is necessary for the conduct of the war, nobody will have any objection. But if one goes about the country-and I have been around to a limited extent in Ontario-one can find evidence of where too much money is being spent and a lot wasted on home defence. I know there are such cases in Toronto. The taxpayer who has his eyes open is complaining on this score to members of parliament. At the same time, some members of our overseas forces are not getting the little pin money increase which they were voted last June.
I do not believe we are getting full value for our money. We have no sovereignty; we have too constantly an eye on Washington,- which seems to be the capital of Canada as regards finance and many other matters. If this sort of thing goes on -there may be some serious developments before next June. Our system of checking expenditures is all antiquated and wrong. You appoint a war expenditures committee to go over the expenditure of this $3,890,000,000, and what do they do? They might just as well never meet for all the reforms they present to the house. The reports are tabled and are never used.
For the supervision of these civil and war expenditures the house depends on two officials, the auditor general and the comptroller of the treasury. They are the only officials who can protect the taxpayer and see that the accounts are properly dealt with and audited, yet they cannot veto a dollar of it.
We might as well admit that we have the dead hand of the treasury in control. The moment you pass this resolution and this bill you are committing this country to an expenditure of $3,890,000,000. Your officials have very little to say about it and little to do beyond putting their seal and stamp on it.

Mr. Chairman.
I understand we are discussing resolution No. 10 of the order paper to authorize the government to guarantee the Canadian National Railways debentures.
No. I must inform the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) that we are discussing resolution No. 3 of the order poper.

Mr. Speaker, our seats are so far removed from the Chair that it is sometimes hard for us to hear what is going on.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Ilsley thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 96, for granting to his majesty aid for national defence and security.

Motion agreed to, bill read the first and second time4 and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Bradette in the chair.
Bill reported.
M-r. ILSLEY moved the third reading of the bill.

I will not detain the passage of the bill for more than half a minute. During the last session,' under the war expenditure bill, I said there was a good deal of discussion of public controls and the officials of the department and it was found that we did not know from day to day, from week to week exactly what these departments and the controls and sub-controls cost the country. A mint of money is being spent like water and there is not a word in the auditor general's report about it. There are a good many of these gentlemen engaged in this control business and while I have respect for them I must point out that many of them are professors and mere academic theorists -who do not know anything about finance. They have had no experience in any competitive business and the result of these controls has been that they have done a good deal of harm to competitive business in Canada, wholesale and retail. They and their orders have ruined a number of storekeepers. I suggest that parliament should be kept better informed. Yesterday one of these gentlemen announced a 75-cent order in connection with coal, over
War Appropriation-Army

the head of parliament, and without any authority whatever. Once you vote these money bills that is the end of it, even if the amount involved is only one-sixth.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 14, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: This is the third and, I hope, the final chapter in the presentation of this statement with respect to the activities of the army during the past year and in the light of what is ahead of us. As I concluded the other evening I indicated that I had a few words to say with regard to the much discussed subject of man-power.
Why the final chapter? Does the minister mean that he does not want further discussion? Is his word the last, the final chapter?

I hope my hon. friend
does not think I am of that mentality*
I hope not.

I do not think the question is really necessary. I am hoping that I can finish before six o'clock. I have a forecast of what are regarded as the estimated total manpower requirements for the three armed services for the fiscal year 1943-44. That estimate is: for the army, 100,000, of which number 75.000 will be for service overseas and 25,000 for service in Canada; the navy, 24,000; the air force, 53,000. The total is 177,000. These figures would represent what I might call the gross intake of the three services during the year in man-power, and the committee will remember that a month and a half have already gone. The 177,000 does not represent, however, the net drain on the man-power of the country, because while these men are being taken into the service a certain number of men are being discharged and are going back into the man-power pool. One can only make an estimate, but to give an idea, I should think that probably the net drain on the man-power pool as a result of this year's 
operations, and if these objectives are reached and these needs called for, would be about
150,000.
What is the total number discharged to date?

Those figures I have not before me at the moment. With regard to man-power, the whole field is primarily for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), but manpower and the obtaining of man-power for the armed services particularly is a joint effort. The Minister of Labour and the national selective service branch are interested in the calling up of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act.

Does that 150,000
cover the three branches?

Yes; army, navy and air force. That 150,000 is the estimate of the net drain on man-power. The Minister of Labour, in connection with his activities in directing national selective service, is also the minister primarily responsible for making the best adjustment of labour employment, so that men will be available-and I am speaking particularly of the armed forces

first, to be called up undter the National Resources Mobilization Act, so that they will be men who will not require to be postponed or to be replaced by others, and second, to volunteer for service in the navy, the army and the air force, or in, other words, so that they can be spared from pressure of their particular occupation. The Minister of Labour's job, the part of it particularly in connection with national selective service, is to help to release these men from their civilian occupations and have them replaced ,if necessary by others not qualified for military service. The navy, the army and the air force are a joint effort, and they have their responsibility in keeping the needs of the service before everyone, concerned, including the public, andJ in vigorously promoting the recruiting of enlistments and cooperating with national selective service and with every agency that can help to release men for service.
I believe it is only in close integration of the activities of these departments that the best results can be obtained, but those are only two of the agencies that have an opportunity to contribute and have responsibility in connection with the provision of man-power. This is a joint effort that cannot be successful without the support of the citizens of Canada. No department and no board can make necessary adjustments in

War Appropriation-Army
man-power, I suggest, with that ideal objective of putting every man and woman where they can serve best, without the help and genuine interest of employers and employees and of the citizens generally.
Here are some of the means which can be taken advantage of whereby men will be available to supply these requirements of which I have spoken. There wit, I am sure, be continuing readjustments in industry to substitute over-age,, under-age and unfit men for men who are eligible for military service. There will be some sort of readjustment in industry to replace men with women as far as that is possible. There will be continuing increase in the training of women to take the place of men, and in that connection there is a particular public responsibility that exists, namely, the continual education of emplojmrs and prospective employees respecting the needs for women in industry as well as in the armed services. There, are many fields into which one could go if one were dealing extensively wfith this particular point. Suffice it to say that it is not simply the idea of asking a woman to go into ani industry. There has to be the training; there has to be the provision of the social services; there has to be the provision of the living accommodation, and! everything that is necessary in order to make the occupation one which a woman might properly undertake and one in respect of which she could make a genuine contribution at this time.
In addition to these adjustments in industry, there is another situation which is just arising non". I should think there would be a shrinkage, as time goes on, in the requirements for men in industry, particularly war industry. The general expansion in war industries has stopped, and I underline the word "general." In most of them the peak has been reached; the feverish production efforts to produce initial equipment are now subsiding, except for some special items such as ships, planes and things of that sort. As my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply intimated the other day, future requirements -will depend more on usage and less on capital requirements. It does look as though production in many lines will be for maintenance and replacement rather than for first equipment. There will be some change-over, of course, but I should think this new condition would be bound to make it possible to undertake comb-outs of men who in the past have been postponed because they were essential in war industry, and in addition it should release men from the non-essential industries.

Has the minister an estimate of the number of men it is expected
will be combed out within the next six months from industries now being closed down, or from changes in production?

No, I have not. That is not a figure I would have; it would be a matter for my colleague the Minister of Labour. The point I should like to register with the committee this afternoon is that when we are discussing the closing down of industry, or the change-over, or the fact that we are going from initial equipment to replacement, so frequently I hear the question asked, "Into what other industry are they going?" I say that my colleagues the Minister of National Defence for Air, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and myself have an idea that some of these men now can be spared to go into the armed services. I point out that in addition to those pools or those sources there is still the class of married men above twenty-five years of age who have not been called as yet, and there is also what we always have, to take into consideration, the natural increase which takes place in the man-power pool of the country resulting from the gross natural accretion each year of about 113,000 young men who reach the age of nineteen. Of course many of these young men are not physically fit, and of course in connection with the available manpower pool for the armed services one has to reipember that while these young men are coming in, at the other end men are becoming forty-six and are going out. I have not the number of those men before me at the moment, but I have in mind that it amounts to something like 67,000 going out as these younger men are coming in. At the same time I wish to point out that our requirements take account of wastage by reason of age and physical unfitness so that those of the 113,000 who are physically fit are available to meet the needs for which we estimate.
Does the air force get first choice among the men who come of age, having regard to the fact that some 60,000 men annually are required for the air force?
There is nothing I know of that gives the air force first choice in connection with the young men who come up.
But the natural consequence would be that the air force would have first choice, would it not? The need for young men in the air force makes that necessary, does it not?

It is a matter of voluntary enlistment; there is no question of first choice. A man enlists in whatever service he prefers. It is possible that the air force may have more
War Appropriation-Army

attraction for some of the younger men, but there is no established priority as between the air force, the army and the navy. The committee will see that getting man-power from these sources calls for the team-work of everyone concerned, and I suggest that this team-work will not be really effective without the conviction that Canada cannot play its full part in helping to win the war unless the navy, the army and the air force are kept constantly supplied with fighting men as well as equipment.
I was going to deal for a moment or two, because I thought perhaps this was the time to do it, with one or two industries which may be said to be competing with the armed forces, and the regulations which are in force respecting them. I refer particularly to agriculture, coal mining, logging and1 base metals. I am sure there has been a feeling in some quarters of this house that the national selective service regulations respecting agriculture vis-a-vis the army were, shall I say, too tough. I want hon. members to see the other side of it, as it is seen by those of us who are concerned with the armed forces; and I should like to remind them that, until the passing of the emergency order in council referred to by my colleague the Minister of Labour, agriculture was the one vocation in the whole country specifically mentioned as being entitled to postponement under certain conditions. Under the provisions with regard to agriculture it was provided that any man who was employed in agriculture on March 24, 1942,-I think that was the date-should be entitled to postponement unless it was established to the satisfaction of the board that he was not essential to agriculture. That action was not taken with regard to any other vocation; and that regulation was administered not by a board which had to do with the armed services nor, as a matter of fact, by a board which had to do with agriculture directly. It was administered by a board presided over by a judge, which was selected by the Department of National War Services at that time and later by the Department of Labour, entirely apart from the military authorities; a board which made its own decisions on the evidence which it procured itself or which was submitted to it by the applicant, by the military people, by the employer or by whoever might be interested in that particular application. I do not think anything could have been fairer than that to agriculture; and I know there have been cases in which the representative of the district officer commanding has felt that considerable latitude was being allowed in connection with some of these applications, in which it was felt that perhaps the army might

have been fairly entitled to the benefit of the services of the individuals. Nevertheless that was the rule, and I think that rule was administered by the boards as fairly as possible having regard to the interests of all concerned; I am sure they were doing their level best to make fair decisions, having regard to the regulations which they were carrying out.
Has the minister the number of men who have been taken from the farms since that order was put through?

I will tell the committee
what I believe-and I think it is a significant figure. This percentage was given to me last December. I understand that of all the applications for postponement made straight across Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, fifty per cent were made on- account of men to be engaged in agriculture. I understand, further, that of those applications made, eighty per cent were granted. I think that is pretty fair treatment by the board for agriculture.
May I say one further word in answer to my hon. friend. I cannot tell him the number of men. I think as a matter of fact one could get the figure, because the Minister of Labour would no doubt have it. I cannot tell the hon. member the number of men who have been given postponements, but I . suggest this, that for each man who has gone from the farms to the armed services, probably two men have gone to industry. I have not the figure 'before me to prove that statement, but I have some information, and I have heard the statement made more than once. In other words, the pull from the farm has not been entirely on account of the armed services, but rather through pressure and attraction of other lines of endeavour, and other lines of war work.

The minister said- that
eighty per cent of those who were asking for postponements were given them. Has he any figure as to the number of these who received temporary postponement and were later called? There were a lot of postponements granted temporarily.

No, I have not. Those
figures are not given, unless we particularly ask for them, but even if we do ask, it would take some time, because a long time is required to make them up. However, I asked for this figure last December with regard to the percentage of postponements on account of agriculture, and the percentage granted.

Has the
minister the figures to substantiate what he

War Appropriation-Army
has said to the effect that two men have gone to industry for every one to the armed services?

The information is obtained from the representatives of district officers commanding. In cases where applications were made for postponement, where the man was, shall I say, the last man or the second to last man on a farm, the question would come up as to where the rest had gone, and generally it was found1-at least this is the information I got-that if there had been a number on the farm, probably two had gone to industry or some similar occupation, as compared with one going into the armed services.
And, remember, I am not finding fault with that. I am only saying that sometimes the army, the navy or the air force is blamed for taking the men off the farms, when as a matter of fact they have gone to places other than farms.
My understanding was that the figures were about fifty-fifty, that of about 400,000 leaving agriculture, 200,000 went to industry and 200,000 went to the armed services.

I would not expect there
were 200,000 from agriculture in the armed services.
One thing more:	Following up that provision as it stands, there was a further provision by means of an interpretative- letter whereby not only did it have to be shown that a man was non-essential- to agriculture, but further than that, even in the event of his being shown to be non-essential to agriculture, where he was working, he was entitled to three months' postponement in order that it might be found out whether some place could be found for him in agriculture.
That is a recent provision.

Yes; that is last January. I mention that to hon. members to let them know that we in the department feel that agriculture has not been unfairly dealt with, and I will not put it stronger than that at the moment, because I think perhaps understatement is preferable.
Then, with regard to coal mining, for a year or more, coal miners have not been encouraged to enlist. They have been deferred as being in essential industry when they have been called up. A request was made some months ago to the army to release men who had been in coal mining, with the
result that the army made an order directing that all men engaged in coal mining should be released, on their applications. Companies were allowed to get in touch with those men, in order that they might be persuaded to go back to their work.
That was voluntary on their part.

Yes; it was voluntary. There was only one condition the army made, namely, that if military exigencies made their services necessary they could not be allowed to go. And it was expressly underlined in the direction that was given that military exigencies had to be real, not fancied. We did not use those exact words, but that is the effect of the order. Those men were given three months' leave.

Has the
minister the figure?

I think it was 1,226. I understand there were about 3,300 miners altogether in the army, but that number would include more than coal miners, alone. The 1,226 in question were the ones who took leave under that order. When the extension was authorized, about 100 of the 1,226 did not ask for further leave, so that at the present time about 1,100 men from the army are in the coal mines. The house has heard to-day respecting- steps which have been taken concerning coal mining in general, having regard to the present emergency.

I should
think the minister's figure is low. My information is that about a thousand miners have enlisted from Cumberland county.

Those are the figures I have. I am talking about skilled coal miners of course, and those are the figures given to me. It may be that a number from that county have enlisted in the air force or the navy. It will be understood that I am talking about the army, alone.
I do not think any distinction has been made. The figure is for the men enlisted from coal -mines in the armed services.

I am talking only about the army. I do not know what the figures for the navy and the air force might be.
Then, with regard to base metal mining, provisions for deferment have -been the same as for coal mining. That is, the -men who were regarded as essential to the industry, those men who might be called skilled, key men, were deferred, when they were called up.
276S
War Appropriation-Army

Then, with respect to logging, that was another call made on the army. It was pointed out that an emergency had developed in the logging industry. We did the same as we had done in connection with the miners, and issued a similar order applying to the Pacific coast area, where the shortage was . alleged to have occurred. The result was that three months leave was given to the men to return to the lumbering industry of British Columbia. I mention these points because, as I have said1 before, I think there is a feeling that the army is tough in these matters. I want hon. members to feel that the army does its best, having regard to its responsibilities. It does feel that the regulations have been fairly generous, or that certainly they have not been unduly harsh in respect of these basic industries.
When the army has to look for men, get them in, train them, and then hand them over to coal mining, lumbering or some other industry, then I submit that the army has been showing at least an endeavour to cooperate, and to try to recognize the need of other agencies.

Do the figures on exemptions include training centres as well as the Canadian army? For example, miners were granted an exemption for three months to return to the mines. Was the minister speaking only of the Canadian active army, or was he speaking of the training centres as well?
I thought I was speaking for the whole command. I think the notice was sent out respecting the whole Pacific comifiand.
Did it cover the training centres also?
I think so. I have not the order here, but I think that is right.
Can the minister say what number went back to the logging industry?

No; I cannot remember now, but I will give my hon. friend the number. I wish just to make this statement and this appeal with regard to man-power. The situation is that for two years everybody has dipped pretty freely and probably too prodigally into the pool of man-power. This year comes the inevitable realization that there is a limit and that the supply is not inexhaustible. I should like to say a word for the army. It has seemed to me that when any agency feels the pinch for manpower, it is the armed forces, and particularly

the army,, which is expected to give back from its ranks. One reason is the fact that the army is in plain sight. It is harder to find the men who have gone into industry. The records are not so complete and hands cannot be laid on them so easily.
The pull of high wages in factories and in plants makes it more difficult to get the men to come back. I submit that these are not really good reasons for drawing men from the army. Canada has undertaken to raise and maintain the strongest and best army we can muster, and we cannot do that [DOT] if the army is to be extended or contracted like an accordion, by pulling men out each time a shortage threatens in some particular line of activity and thinking we can put them back again and go on as if all the while they had been, carrying on their military duties.
Speaking for the army, I would not be in as strong a position, if the army had not itself tried to practise economy in man-power. But the army has made some pretty drastic cuts, and we are keeping at it morning, noon and night. I know there has been belt-tightening in industry, both primary and secondary, but we must remember that the armed forces are still in numbers far below the army of agriculture, which is probably a million or more, or the army of munitions and supply, which is probably nine hundred thousand to a million, directly and indirectly. The army, navy and air force put together aggregate only a little over 700,000. I know it is uncomfortable to go shorthanded. It is uncomfortable and tough for the farmer, and the farms have done well in supplying men. But I think it is true that, taking Canada as a whole, for every man who has left the farm or the woods or the mines to join the armed forces, two men have gone into industry and other civilian occupations. It is uncomfortable and dislocating for the employer in industry, and I yield to no one in appreciation of the accomplishments of these three years in producing munitions, but men over age or unfit physically for the fighting forces, and women, can produce munitions. It is tough and uncomfortable for the storekeeper, the office man and the housewife to go shorthanded, but physically fit men for the armed forces, and women to take their places in the army and in industry, are needed.
I do not believe that the pattern for the army which parliament has authorized is one which cannot be lived up to, provided we are willing to make the necessary adjustments in our way of living and working. Combined armed forces of less than three-quarters of a

War Appropriation-Army
million out of a population, of 11,500,000 is not an undue proportion. I think we must realize that besides equipment, it will need all the men that all the allies can muster, even counting the man-power reserves of Russia and China. I think we must realize, too, that while the war cannot be won without the team-work of all three services, land armies are bound to be the final instrument for victory in this war. Surely this has been amply proved in Russia and North Africa. This means that all the united nations, Canada included, must have the strongest and best army that they can raise.
Neither in victory loans nor in materials nor in men has the real pinch come. We ration tea, sugar, gasoline, rubber and clothing; we create priorities for this, that and the other thing, but nobody in this house or this country has gone hungry or cold on this account. In [DOT]man-power we are really just beginning to be rationed now. The question is: Shall we see it through, or shall we, as it becomes harder to get men or as it becomes difficult to get material, simply throw up our hands and say, "It is too uncomfortable and too inconvenient, let us lower our sights and have less bother." I leave that question with the committee and with the country. If we have the stamina of the men of the navy, the army and the air force, there will be only one response, that we are going to stick it just the way they are sticking it in connection with the job they are doing.
I have mentioned man-power because it affects the army. I think the Minister of Labour intends shortly to make a statement with regard to man-power in general, but I have referred to it in order to indicate some of the sources and some of the ways in which I think members of the House of Commons and the Department of Labour and other departments can help in connection with the making available of these men.
Would the minister indicate the extent to which the army itself has been able to replace men with women to release men for active service?

We have about 10,000 in the Canadian Women's Army Corps, of which probably 8,000 have replaced men. In the home war establishments, I would say that sixty per cent of the general service personnel are either thirty-five years of age or in a category unsuitable for overseas service under present practice. That gives my hon. friend some idea. I may say that in one district alone a saving of between 1,000 and 1,100 men has been achieved by a readjustment and
reduction of establishments and by a general reassorting in order to have work done by, say one and a half men which was formerly done by two men. A committee from headquarters is travelling constantly throughout the country doing nothing other than dealing with man-power problems. They are consulting with the district officers commanding and making reports. They stay in the district and go over the establishments in an endeavour to see just what can be done in carrying on with fewer men.
The minister mentioned that sixty per cent of the positions had been taken over by low category men.
That is the home war establishments.

Will that
process be extended?
You could not extend it to operational troops.
I am thinking of the home war establishments.

That is the place where we are making the greatest saving. As I explained the other day, these cover headquarters and services of all sorts, such as supplies and services of that kind, instructional staff, administrative staff and so on. These are the things in connection with which we are endeavouring to save as much as possible.

To what
extent can the process be extended, or has the limit pretty well been reached?

It is being extended in each district. Of course it is being constantly watched and dealt with by this committee which is doing nothing else.
Here I should like to put on record a word with regard to the Canadian Women's Army Corps. It fits in with the questions which have just been asked. The Canadian Women's Army Corps have given us perhaps the greatest satisfaction we have had in connection with operations for the fiscal year just closed. A year ago the Canadian Women's Army Corps numbered about 2,000; to-day it numbers about 10,000. At the present time we have in the United Kingdom about 400 members of this corps, and we have 100 in the United States.
In England the organization which corresponds with the C.W.A.C. is the Auxiliary Territorial Service. We were fortunate this year in having a visit from Major-General Jean Knox, the commanding officer of the A.T.S. General Knox gave two strenuous
War Appropriation-Army

months in travelling across Canada and visiting the various C.W.A.C. detachments. She conferred with the officers, addressed public meetings and discussed the whole problem of women in the armed services. Her tact, experience and judgment were of marked benefit. I wish to put on Hansard publicly our grateful acknowledgment to 'her and to Sir James Grigg, Secretary of State for War, and Lieutenant-General Sir Ronald Adams, the Adjutant-General, for their cooperation in making her visit possible. Our girls got a great deal of good out of General Knox's visit, and a sequence of that was that a number of our senior officers went to England to learn at first hand the methods of operation there. Most of them took an officers' administrative course, and some of them a field security course under A.T.S. direction. Most of these officers have now returned and the corps is getting the benefit of their experience.
McGill university agreed that we could make use of the whole of Macdonald college to provide the first training centre for this corps. An equally fine cooperative spirit was shown by the Alberta government, which gave us the use of the Agricultural college at Vermilion, Alberta. At the present time the non-commissioned officers and cooks all go to Macdonald college. At Vermilion basic training is carried on. We found the necessity for further basic training, and we converted what was the basic training centre for men at Kitchener to basic training for the women's corps. At the present time we have a total capacity at Vermilion of from 350 to 450 a month, and at Kitchener a capacity of something like 1,200.
With regard to the activities of the C.W.A.C., when we started out we thought the opportunities for operation of the corps were extremely limited, and they were divided roughly into four groups: clerical, motor drivers and mechanics, canteen assistants, dietetics-that is cooks and waitresses. But now the occupations for women tradesmen are almost as great in number as those of men. To give an idea of the variety, at the present time women of the C.W.A.C. are taking the following courses: night vision testers; provost duties; radio operators; photography; clerical and stenography; kinetheodolite-that is handling the technical equipment for anti-aircraft guns-ordnance.
In the vocations for C.W.A.C. personnel there are thirty-two different listings under the following main headings: medical, clerical, kitchens and messing, dental, draughting, automotive, signals, storemen, sundry. At the beginning of the fiscal year we had practically no separate accommodation for the C.W.A.C. personnel, but now there are barracks in no

fewer than thirty-seven localities, accommodating over 9,000 officers and other ranks.
I think the best compliment which can be paid to the efficiency and usefulness of the corps is the demand which is made for its services. I can say this for the C.W.A.C., that there is no corps in the army the demand for which has so exceeded the supply. Canadian military headquarters overseas did not at first receive with any particular enthusiasm the suggestion that some of the personnel might be sent overseas to release fit men for more active duty. Eventually two detachments went over, numbering in all about 400. Almost immediately after they got settled down to work a request came for 3,000. We have not been able to supply that as yet. Almost every district and certainly every branch of the service are clamouring for more C.W.A.C. personnel. The corps has more than justified our most optimistic expectations; Canadians as a whole are proud of the smartness of these young women and the way they are turned out, and I am sure we are gratified at the efficient service they are giving.
How is the recruiting for the corps coming along? What is the quota?
About 700 a month are coming in just now.
What is the quota?

We want more than that. All three services are recruiting at the present time. We have accommodation now for about 1,200 a month, but we shall have accommodation for 1,400 a month when some increases at Vermilion are finished. If by quota my hon. friend means the requirements of the three services, I would say that the requirements for women in the three armed forces for the present fiscal year are in the neighbourhood of 30,000.
I mean for the women's army. The quota is about 1,200, is it?
We shall have accommodation for 1,400 soon, if we can get them.
And you are getting about 700?
Yes.
Of the 10,000 which the minister mentioned a little while ago, how many are officers in the C.W.A.C.?
They would not need any more officers than the army itself.

It is part of the army.

There are 349 officers and 9,640 other ranks. That is as of March 27. About four per cent are officers.

In labour work we advocate that women who do the same work as men should get the same pay. Is that the, situation in the C.W.A.C.? Do women, who replace men in administrative work receive the same rate of pay as the men?

No, they do not. The women began with a proportion of the pay of the men. There is a proposal being put forward now-I am not saying that it has been accepted-that while the basic rate for men and women will remain the same, when a woman goes into one of the trades, the trades pay will be the same as for men.

It is gratifying to hear the minister speak so highly of the C.W.A.C. They are pleased to have the opportunity to serve their country in this way. Has the minister given any thought to the question that was brought before him some time ago of dependents' allowance for women in the armed services? That is still a question very much to the fore.

That question has been very much to the fore, also the question raised by the hon. member for Fort William, both of which are under consideration now. Even if the minister had not wanted to give any thought to the matter, I may tell the hon. member for Edmonton East that he could not have helped doing so because it has been forcibly brought to his attention.
Another branch of the army that deserves special mention is the reserve army. I know I am now talking to some members of the reserve army who probably know a great deal more about it than I do. The reserve army has in the last year taken on a new interest in life as a result of its year's work. The reserve army has been given a definite place in the defence plans of this country. In writing to a citizen not very long ago I said, "The purpose and password of the reserve army is preparedness." Some of its objects were to provide training facilities and opportunities for citizens who want to be prepared, but who still have civil responsibilities, to fit themselves for service if required. One of the outstanding features of the reserve army is that a citizen can serve in two capacities. He may be serving on a war job in the daytime and then serve on another war job in the evening, preparing himself in case the worst should come.
The minister, I assume, will give us figures showing the numbers in the reserve army.

I will give the figures, but I had not intended to do so now. I can tell my hon. friend that, roughly, there are a hundred thousand in the reserve army. I have not the exact figures here.
Another task is to prepare primarily for community and local defence if the need should come, and to provide possibly for other service in Canada in case a serious national emergency should arise. One of the most important roles of the reserve army is to provide trained men as volunteers for the active army, not only directly from the reserve army ranks, but also indirectly, through responsible citizens giving genuine leadership, by training themselves and impressing their neighbours, first, with the fact that this country is in the war to the finish; second1, that the war is a long way from being won; third, that preparation is necessary for any eventuality either here or overseas.
In connection with this matter of recruiting, the figures I have show that for December, January, February and March an average of over seven hundred men a month enlisted from the reserve army.
The reserve army is officered by citizens selected from leading positions in civil life and from reserves of ex-officers. The training of the reserve army has been, I believe, very much improved by reason not only of the new syllabi which have been adopted but also by means of the amount of equipment we have been able to issue.
I do not wish to take more time in connection with this, because I have a number of other subjects to deal with. But I cannot refrain from expressing my admiration and appreciation of the turn-outs of the reserve army which I have seen. I am sure that they have been just as good as the turn-outs of the active army; and that is'saying a good deal for both of them. The keenness which has been shown, particularly by the veteran who perhaps is too old to take a positon in the active army, standing almost alongside the young fellow of seventeen or eighteen years of age, with the manager of a department store beside the dentist, or beside somebody in charge of a radio station; all doing their jobs, taking their training as if they really liked it, doing it because they feel it is worth while setting an example to the people of this country and imbuing them with the spirit that this country is at war-to this I would pay very sincere tribute. I thank the citizens of this country for their support of the reserve army. I know that quite a number of members of this house have set a good example and, if I may say so, have received some benefit
War Appropriation-Army

themselves from joining the reserve army. Veterans of the last war have given their experience and services to make it a success. It is a great stimulation to see these old soldiers and responsible citizens unite with the youths who are equally enthusiastic in willingness to back up the active army. They have been willing to forego time and comfort in order to be prepared. They have built a sound organization which can be relied on as an essential part of our defence plan.
We have noted with the greatest appreciation and gratification the rapid growth of the reserve army this year, and are taking active steps toward giving them additional operational responsibilities, particularly in the coastal areas. This will apply especially to infantry and anti-aircraft units.
Another organization, which used to be my favourite when I was in this position ten or fifteen years ago, and one on which whole debates on national defence estimates occurred, is the cadets.
Before the minister goes on, would he prefer that we ask him questions concerning the reserve army at a later time, after he finishes his whole statement?

Yes; if my hop. friend is so kind as to agree. I suggested to the committee that I might put the statement on record as consecutively as possible; then there would be subjects which would suggest themselves to the committee, and I would try to be prepared to answer their questions.
The cadets this year have organized and started out on a line of activity which I think will be exceedingly useful. They are tremendously keen. His Majesty the King has been so gracious as to accept the appointment of Colonel-in-Chief of the cadets; and he was good enough also to allow the use of the word "royal"; so that to-day the boys belong to the Royal Canadian Army Cadets, ' and they have as Coloneldn-Chief His Majesty the King. They have been provided with uniforms, half the cost of which they pay themselves, the other half being paid for by the country. That the uniform has a good deal to do with the smartness of the soldier and the attractiveness of the service, there is no doubt. They have made the very best use of it. I do not think I have seen any smarter turn-out of the youth of Canada than the parade of one of the cadet units of this city that I had the opportunity of visiting a few weeks ago.
There are about ninety-four thousand cadets altogether, about fifty per cent of them being

seniors and fifty per cent juniors. Those over fifteen years of age are classed as seniors.
In addition to getting a uniform, they are receiving equipment. They have been given a new syllabus of training. We have tried to make it interesting as well as practical. We have endeavoured to make the syllabus such as would develop the skills of the new type of soldier in connection with the duties and the weapons which the modern soldier has to know about. We have tried to develop a syllabus so that the sense of discipline is based on knowledge, on logic, on enthusiasm and on pride. It is a syllabus which will give them a broader understanding of the responsibilities of Canadian citizenship generally.
The reserve army is assisting in a very particular way in connection with the training and development of the boys in the cadet corps. Many of the cadet units are attached to units of the reserve army. Many of the cadet units, as hon. members know, are in the schools; some of them are sponsored by clubs and other civic organizations; but they are all welded together into the Royal Canadian Army Cadets, and I must say that they are doing a good job.. Mr. Churchill the other evening, when speaking of the home guards, said, "with them came the lads of seventeen already trained in the army cadet corps"; and the boys of Canada are coming right along with the reserve army. We hope that their next step will be to go into the active army.
I wish to express my particular appreciation for the great help which has been given by the education departments of the provinces in connection with what has been a rather delicate and difficult situation with regard to the cadet movement, because, as the committee knows, there are air cadets and sea cadets as well. But I believe that difficulties have been ipretty well taken care of. We have had the greatest cooperation from the departments of education, from, the principals, the teachers and the cadet instructors. We try to qualify these instructors in every way possible by giving them special courses in connection with the work they will be doing with the boys.
While I am speaking of the boys, there is one more activity in the army which I should like to mention, namely, the course which we started quite lately for vocational training of boys. It was a development of this year; indeed all these things of which I am speaking are really developments of this year. I do not propose to deal with basic and advanced training centres, much as I should like to do so.

War Appropriation-Army
The idea of these boys' vocational training is to give lads of seventeen and) eighteen a head start, as they say, in trades training for the army. It provides them with trades training which will be valuable not only in the army but in civil life as well. It is open to boys who have completed grade nine. They send in an application to the principal, andi the principal sends in a report to the district trades training officer, who decides whether the candidates ought to be brought in for interview. Those who are accepted enlist, provided of course that they have the consent of their parents. First, they take at least two weeks' military training; then they go to technical and) vocational schools which have been established in western, central and eastern Canada. The courses last about ten months; and) during the course, in addition to their trades training, they have military training for nine hours a week. These young soldiers receive boys' pay, seventy cents a day, until they are seventeen and a half years old; they then receive sob diers' pay; and none, of course, go overseas until they reach nineteen years of age. They get training as fitters, mechanics, electricians, draftsmen, artificers and other trade specialists, and the object is to provide an opportunity for every boy to get that education which he would receive between the time he would normally leave school and the time he goes into the army.
In connection with selection of officers we have this year adopted a system w'hich is an innovation so far as Canada is concerned. It is not like the system in either England or the United States, but we felt that it was necessary if we were to have uniformity in the training of junior officers. We had boys coming in from different districts going to Brockville or Gordon Head, recommended by their commanding officers as fit and1 suitable as officer cadets to take up the Brockville or Gordon Head course. The general principles of qualification were laid down, but apparently there was a wide difference between these standards and the actual attainments of the men who came to Brockville. The result was that there were failures, and some of the boys got discouraged, although I may observe that the percentage of failures was remarkably small. It was our opinion, however, with respect to these future leaders of men, that they ought to have a preliminary look-over, so to speak, before being sent to Brockville or Gordon Head. We have therefore established two officers selection and appraisal centres, one in the east and one in the west. The eastern centre at Three Rivers
had as commanding officer Brigadier Foster, who has now taken the position of defence projects commissioner in the west, his place having been taken by Brigadier General MoCuaig. Brigadier Archambault is associate chairman of the board. In the west, either this week or next week, we shall have in charge of the work at Chilliwack, Brigadier Wilson, who previously was in charge of the Gordon Head officers training centre.

Are these
travelling schools?

These are not travelling
schools. The boys live as closely as possible under the observation of the senior officers. There is an officer from each corps-artillery, infantry, ordnance and so on. They put the boys through various tests and have interviews with them with a view to ascertaining their capabilities and their objectives in life. In short, they take a fatherly and intimate interest in them, and appraise them, as it were, to find out exactly what the boys are best fitted for. The object is to help a boy, first, to suggest what arm of the service he could best serve in; second, to give some preliminary idea of the responsibility with which he will be charged in the future as an officer.

Is there
an educational standard or test?
Yes; I believe it is grade nine.
The reason why I ask is that Major Rouse from my'city is doing this work at Three Rivers.

The object is, first, to
give an idea of the responsibility of officers; second, to attain some uniform standard of qualifications; and third, to advise with regard to the adaptability of the boys to different branches of the service. Consideration had to be given to the boy who would not make the grade. If he went to Brockville or to Gordon Head, he might be ploughed and there would be a black mark against him. The idea was, therefore, to give that boy an idea of the further training he should undergo and to make him feel that he was not being sent back as turned, down for good. Rather it was to impress upon him the importance of obtaining further training inasmuch as he was setting out upon an important vocation in life.
