No. So far they have
not. The school has worked well so far. It has been in operation for only three months, but the reports are extremely promising. There has been a classification of men: the top, 50 per cent; the next, 30 per cent; the next, 10 per cent, and 10 per cent.

These young men are
chosen by the commanding officers from the units?
Yes.

Are they
no longer taken from the C.O.T.C., from the universities?
Yes.

Then
they are not always from the units?

I had in mind the commanding officer of the C.O.T.C. This brings me to the point raised by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). As soon as the Chilliwack centre is established, what we shall be putting into effect is this, that any boy may make application to his commanding officer, if he thinks he can make the grade, for a commission. The commanding officer may not favour the application, but he cannot send it back. He must forward it to the board for consideration, and the board will have the boy come to them, or cause him to be examined by some board of their own, apart from the commanding officer. The object is to give the chap who has ambition an opportunity, on his own, to obtain a detached appraisal of his ability instead of having him entirely within the confines of a particular unit of which he may be a member. The new system stresses leadership particularly, and that is well brought out by the officers, whom we are sending there to be in charge. We also stress the qualities of character and practical knowledge as well as of military attainments, because they can get their military attainments by training.

Mr. Chairman, there were two or three other special activities that I thought might be of interest to the committee, though I do not intend to take very long with any of them. The training of officers, as the committee knows, is perhaps

one of the most important activities that we carry on, and I want to give the figures for Brockville and Gordon Head, which may be of interest. Up to the end of April of this year we graduated from these training centres 11,686 officers, including 669 who graduated not from Brockville and Gordon Head direct but from ad hoc training centres wdiich we set up in order to take care of additional needs while we were carrying on construction at these two centres. That construction wTill be finished very shortly, and then we shall have accommodation at Brockville for some 8.000 officers per annum and at Gordon Head for some 2,900.
I think I can say that the schools have done well; I think, too, they have had excellent material with which to work. At Gordon Head the cadets naturally are practicallj' all English-speaking Canadians, but I am sure it is a matter of satisfaction to know that at Brockville French-Canadians and English-Canadians in the proportion of about one to three have graduated during the last year. I do not think there could be any better evidence of a willingness, desire and determination, to make some united contribution to this war than is shown by the cordial association of these young men at Brockville and by the comradeships, the foundations of which are laid at that institution. Last year we had just started a new experiment in the way of pre-training for French-Cana.dian cadets at St. Jerome. That school began operating in February, 1942, and the output for the year has been approximately 1,000 cadets. As the committee will remember, we have had young French-Canadians selected by civilian committees. They went, first to St. Jerome, where they were given a month's basic training. If they progressed well and showed promise and a desire to carry on and enlisted, they were put into what we called the cadet wing at St. Jerome, where they were given another month's training. The training is not altogether similar but is generally in line with the idea of the new selection centres at Three Rivers and Chilliwack which I mentioned just before six o'clock, except that the French-Canadian boys have been at St. Jerome. They go to this precadet wing, where they have this month of training. This gives them some idea of the associations and the responsibilities of officers; it gives them some preparation which helps to overcome the bit of handicap which these boys naturally would feel in going to a school where most of the boys were English. Generally it gives them a

War Appropriation-Army
foundation' which is of extreme value when they go to Brockville and meet their English-speaking confreres. That school has been a success from the very start. It will be tied in, as a matter of fact, with the selection centre at Three Rivers, of which I spoke this afternoon.
Another innovation which was initiated this year and which I think is well worth noting, is our organization with regard to improvements in equipment, the development of mechanical and technical devices. There is always a great urge and a great rush in the urgent necessity of producing standard types of weapons, and that rush and urge very often obscure the necessity for constant effort to improve. The army research man is not always very popular with the production man. The production man gets set; he wants to get mass production going and is not too enthusiastic about any suggestion of change. Nevertheless changes have to be made; we are in a gruelling race with the axis for efficiency and more efficiency in connection with equipment, and we have set up two agencies which I think have done extremely useful work. First, we have formed a branch of the general staff called the directorate of staff duties (weapons). He represents the ultimate consumer; that is, the man in the field. He has to do with quantities of weapons, but he also has to do with something else, perhaps his most interesting activity, namely, w;ith developments and improvements of weapons. He is in constant communication with the army overseas to see what needs have arisen for new types of weapons and for the improvement of existing types. He is a clearing-house for new ideas which come from the army anywhere in the way of new or improved weapons, and it is the job of his section to appraise the probable usefulness of an idea which is suggested, assuming that it can be produced.
It is not very much good having a clearinghouse of ideas unless one can have somebody produce the pilot models or the mock-ups in order to find out whether or not they will work. Therefore it will be remembered that just about a year ago the army technical development board was formed under the chairmanship of the master-general of the ordnance; that was at the time General McNaughton was here. That board is tied in with representatives of munitions and supply and national research as well as the army. Its job is to take the needs of the army and the ideas which have been presented and suggested and, if I may put it in this way, to farm them out either to the national research council, to some other government organization or to
private industry, in an endeavour to have models designed' and built to see if the work required can be done. It may give a job to some particular commercial firm; it may go to the national research laboratories or to the army workshops, but the job of that board is to see that somebody does it and that ideas do not simply get pigeon-holed, as I am sorry to say is sometimes the situation.
Just to show that the activities of this board are not merely theoretical, there have been instances already of changes made which have shown its usefulness. I cannot give details of the weapons, but I can give the characteristics of weapons which have been improved or changed. Take the matter of range, for instance, the range of projectiles. In one case the range of a standard weapon was increased by 25 per cent by improving the projectile. That design has now been accepted. In another case it looks as though the development will increase the range not by 25 per cent but by 300 per cent, and the prototype embodying the new design is now in the United Kingdom under trial. In another case I remember a heavier weapon of a certain type was needed. That has been developed and the prototypes are under trial; there again the range of the projectile was more than doubled. Then several ideas came in for heavy mobile mountings for a standard weapon; those were perfected and the trials carried out, and orders for the new mountings are now in. The muzzle velocity of another weapon was increased by 200 per cent; the rate of fire of still another weapon was doubled, and pilot models are now under test in the United Kingdom. In another instance the design for a multiple mounting, namely a mounting from which the weapons fire in parallel, was perfected, and that has been passed.
These are some of the things that have been done. Needless to say, there are many others which are under development; and while the army organization has been the means of pooling these ideas and getting some practical action in connection with them, full credit must go to the Department of Munitions and Supply and to the national research council for the rapid strides that have been made in this very important field of weapon development. What we have tried to do is to make use of the very best scientific, engineering and industrial brains in Canada, for the purpose of seeing to it that we have the very best types, the most improved types of weapons that can be produced.
Another development which I know is interesting is that of the formation of the paratroop battalion, the authorization of

which took place just a year ago on Dominion day. This, of course, does not represent a large force. They worked in close cooperation with our own master-general of the ordnance, and a great deal of valuable information was secured.	.
The vice-adjutant general recently returned from a visit to our troops at Fort Benning, and the report he brought back with regard to that battalion of ours was most gratifying. Perhaps some hon. members saw the paratroops in Ottawa the other day, when they marched in the victory loan parade, and I am sure that any hon. member, or any person outside the house who saw them would have reason to be proud of that very representative paratroop unit.

There is one other battalion of a somewhat similar nature about which I should like to say a word. Not much is said about it. I refer to the half composite battalion, known as the first special service force, which is now at Helena, Montana. I refer to that half of the battalion which is Canadian. It is a composite battalion, with a United States officer in command and a Canadian officer as second in command. It is formed of picked men who are skilled in parachute and marine landings, and in moimtain and desert warfare, and is being trained for special work. It is the

British commando, plus, becavise it has parachute and marine landing abilities, as well as ability in mountain and desert warfare. The Canadian troops include both officers and men, but the force is actually one body without any special Canadian or United States wing or section.
From now on, will all paratroops be trained at Shilo?

I have said nothing about the training schools or the courses they are giving, or anything about the eighty-seven training establishments. While I give credit to the officers who have been so zealous and so faithful in the conduct of all these lines of activity, at the same time I wish to say a special word with regard to transportation, It is something which is not very much in the public eye, but which is vitally important in connection with the organization and administration of an army. The laconic announcement that appears from time to time in the newspapers that another troopship has arrived overseas, bearing Canadian units and Canadian reinforcements, makes very little impression upon the minds of most of us. Most people do not realize much of what is involved in the steps preceding the time when that particular group of individuals steps on the boat at the dockside.. The details of those last few days require most meticulous planning and attention.
Before the draft is ready, medical examination, documentation, arrangements for leave and completion of clothing and equipment must be attended to. Then come the train

orders, the transportation and security arrangements in, transit, and the timing of the arrival of trains with the time of arrival of the troopship. Arrangements for the disembarkation and security arrangements at the dockside and on the ship, the space allocation and embarkation, are activities of which little is known and less is appreciated by the public.
In the last war everybody knew when a troop train was going through. Everyone flocked to the stations, and with cheers and bands welcomed the troops, and sped them on their way. The whole country had this visible evidence that we were in the war. Nowadays no one knows the time of the moving of these troops. Trainload after trainload moves in secrecy from various centres in Canada, all heading toward the port of embarkation. That takes planning.
I just wish to pay my tribute, not only to the departmental officers, but also to the railway managements, the operating staffs and the running crews of our two great railway systems. They have done a magnificent job in these days of overloaded rolling stock and congested trackage, amid all weather conditions and under the necessity of meeting almost instantly changing schedules on account of alterations in shipping arrangements. Their task has none of the glamour and none of the limelight of service which the public sees, but they give their best with a patience, a devotion and an efficiency 'which can only be, fully realized by those who know of the burdens which they carry, and the difficulties under which they work.
I shall not trouble the committee with further detail of departmental administration, except to mention the medical service, which has a very heavy job, and the organization of which has made remarkable strides in the past year.
Then, a final word with regard to the programme in 1943-44 for the Canadian army overseas. As is usually the case in these matters, one can say least regarding that which is perhaps of the most interest. The committee will not expect me to speculate as to what might take place in this year, as to what operations may develop, where they will be launched, or what the objectives will be. Any discussion of that kind would embarrass not only our own staffs, but those of the allied nations with whose fortunes and activities ours are locked up. What Canada wants to be sure of is that we are fully informed regarding the plans of those who have the direction of the war strategy, and particularly as they affect employment of Canadians, and that we are ready to participate in them when the zero hour strikes.
The army commander is in constant touch with the chief of the imperial general staff with regard to plans. The chief of the general staff here has been in the United Kingdom very recently and has had an opportunity of full discussion both with the army commander and with the war office.
With respect to armaments and equipment of our overseas forces, I can say that the situation has improved greatly during the past year and continues to improve in spite of the large demands from the active theatres. The committee will appreciate that army requirements run into thousands of items. In the case of most of these items we are not only equipped up to establishment but have substantial reserves. In the case of only a few is there an establishment deficiency, but these can be rapidly filled except where there is a universal shortage of supplies affecting all the armies of the united nations. All steps possible have been taken to equip the units and formations of the Canadian army overseas ready to undertake any task that may be assigned to them, but of course it must be understood that each task may require special preparation in the way of organization, rehearsal and equipment. I am confident that Canadians are in position to adapt themselves to any operation as quickly and efficiently as any troops in the United Kingdom.
I am not announcing any new formations for 1943-44. To put it simply, the Canadian contribution to the 1943 overseas programme is primarily' to maintain our forces overseas by replacements of men and equipment and by maintaining adequate reserves for the field forces which may be employed from time to time. We cannot tell, of course, what the exact requirements will be; that must depend on the operations which are to be undertaken. But we estimate, as I have said already, that to cover all contingencies our objective should be an intake, for the twelve-month period, of about 75,000 men for overseas service and about 25,000 men for Canadian service. The equipment situation is well in hand; but, as I have indicated, part of our task for the year will include keeping equipment fully up to date and maintaining adequate reserves.
That, programme does not take long to state, but the committee will appreciate that its brevity is in no way a measure of its importance; far from it. The large increase in the amounts allotted to the army in this resolution are mainly to make provision for activities which the year before us may bring. The battle of North Africa is over after six months of the most spectacular, the fastest-moving, the most relentless and the hardest-hitting offensive ever seen. But we must remember that that battle began over two
War Appropiiation-Army

years ago. The long hoped-for climax was made possible by two major victories. First, there was the glorious advance of the eighth army under the magnificent leadership of General Montgomery and the excellent cooperation between Montgomery's land and air forces. Second, there was the combined operation which began when United States and British forces landed in North Africa and tirelessly and persistently and not without hard fighting forced a debacle last week which must have caused Hitler more chagrin, more humiliation and more impotent rage than even the relief of Stalingrad.
These victories have shown that in brilliant planning and valiant fighting, both leaders and men are superb. Our field organization has proved to be sound, and our armament and equipment have matched and surpassed anything that our enemies have produced. The victories in North Africa, in Russia and in the southern Pacific are far-reaching in their effect; but, as has been said so many times, we must not overestimate the results. These victories have all been part of the preparatory, not the decisive phase of this war. Our armies, other than the Red army, have not yet secured even a foothold on the continent of Europe. Tunisia is not a stopping-place.
The year ahead looks like a year of action. If it is, Canadians will be in the thick of the events for which plans and preparations have long been under way. The Canadian army overseas has already carried out one of the most trying assignments that can come to fighting men, namely, the job of training and working month after month and year after year getting ready to strike and at the same time holding the line against possible attack by air, sea and land. In those dangerous days of 1940 our first division was a strong bastion in the none too rugged bulwarks of Britain. The second division joined them in the fall of 1940, and each year we have dispatched more divisions and more units to be ready to take Canada's share in land operations wherever they are needed. As a distinguished Canadian has put it, they have been the king's bodyguard on the-bridge of freedom.
These men have kept alert; they have maintained their spirit. An officer who came back a few days ago told me that never before has the .Canadian army been more ready, more determined and more keen than it is now after three years of waiting. That in itself is a great achievement for men who have separated themselves from homes and families for so long, men who have just the same ambitions in civil life as you and I, men who took on soldiering not because they preferred it but

because it was the highest duty of a citizen. These soldiers of ours have worked tirelessly to fit themselves for battle. They are well led, and their equipment is of the best. They are on a front which in all likelihood will prove to be the decisive front of the war. They may fight on that front or on some other. They may fight as an army or in separate formations. But wherever they are, they will be a power to be reckoned with, just as Canadians were twenty-five years ago.
The money to be provided by the bill which will be based upon this resolution represents, so far as the dollar sign can express it, the might which the Canadian people will put behind our men in this offensive. But the dollar sign is just a symbol. Translated into fighting power, it means men and guns and tanks and munitions of war. It means the spirit of self-denial and of unflinching perseverance. This year more than ever Canadians at home will suffer real inconvenience and probably some discomfort. But these are trivial troubles compared with the sacrifices which face our sailors, soldiers and airmen. They challenge us to see it through. They challenge us to a redoubled effort until the job is done. Success depends on us just as much as it does on them. If that is so, the nearer that those of us at home can come to matching the steadiness and the enthusiasm of our fighting men, the surer will be the victory and the shorter will be the war.
This statement may be regarded as having been all too long, but there was a great deal of ground to cover. It is at best, a very sketchy resume of the activities of the Canadian army during the past year, having regard particularly to the programme which we set out for ourselves, both in Canada and overseas, the activities which have taken place and what is ahead of us. I submit it to the committee for whatever use it may prove to hon. members. I would assume that members of the committee will want to deal with this matter as if we were in the estimate stage, and that we shall endeavour to make it our objective to give all possible attention to the items which were set out in Hansard by the Minister of Finance, the break-down for the army, so that we may as far as possible ensure an orderly discussion and, I hope, accelerate and facilitate the procuring and production of information.

The minister was not

There can be no doubt whatever that the Canadian people and the members of this

house are entitled to a definite assurance from the ministry that there are and will be sufficient reinforcements to keep all the units of Canada's army up to fighting strength. That assurance has not been given by the Minister of National Defence. He has talked all around it in his statement, but has given no definite assurance that Canada's army will be adequately reinforced. Events will prove whether or not we have sufficient reinforcements. But the responsibility for adequate reinforcements rests right on the shoulders of the ministry. So much for reinforcements.
One other question with regard to the overseas army which I think should be considered carefully by the members of the committee is this: Is the Canadian army overseas to be thrown into battle as an army without the units first having had a chance to get battle experience? Canadians overseas have been given very little opportunity to get battle experience. Some of them, a comparatively small number, did get such experience at Dieppe, but of the number who got that battle experience very few came back from Dieppe. Many hundreds of Canadians, unfortunately, were left on the beach there, and the Canadian prisoners lost at Dieppe number, I believe, almost as many as all the men that were lost by Canada as prisoners during the last war. Casualties were out of all proportion to the number of troops engaged. One cannot praise too highly the valour of the Canadian troops; and in that connection, residents of my city of Vancouver are very proud of the valour of their own Colonel Merritt, who commanded the South Saskatchewan regiment and was awarded the Victoria Cross, upon a citation which I have never seen surpassed in connection with any award to any Canadian. But why should the people who planned that action receive such praise? Why should Dieppe be treated as a great victory? I saw at close quarters some of these "victories" in the last war, in which several hundred or several thousand men were sacrificed. It is not good1 enough, in this second world war, that Canadians should be thrown away by the hundreds unless the plans have been most carefully laid and most carefully carried out. In my opinion the minister went much too far and made much too extravagant statements with regard to this action at Dieppe. He said on Friday last, as reported in Hansard, at'page 2690:
The losses were heavy

Certainly there can be no dispute about that.
[Mr. Green.)
-but although the price was great, when history comes to be written I believe it will be recorded that Dieppe did a service of untold benefit not only on the Russian front and later in North Africa, but to the cause of the united nations generally.
He went on:
It was practically the beginning of the offensive.
Then he excelled himself in these words:
Some day it may well be considered as having sown the seeds of our final victory.
That assertion, I am afraid, is the result of a vivid imagination. I suggest that, rather than exaggerate this action as has been done, and paean it as a great victory, we should be examining the methods which were used in planning it and make sure that those who planned it deserve to continue as leaders of our troops overseas.
Let me now come back to the question of battle training for our troops. There has been much talk of the Canadian army forming the spearhead of the invasion of the continent. That has, of course, a glorious sound; but it would mean, if the Canadian army were to be used as a spearhead at the present time, putting a force of five divisions which has never fought as an army, which has never been in action as a unit, against battle-hardened German troops sitting behind fortifications. It would entail far heavier casualties, as those of us who were in the last war know, than if the units of the army had had battle experience, and if, also, their commanders had had battle experience; because, remember, in a war commanders gain battle experience-unfortunately -at the cost of the lives of troops.
The situation was shown clearly, I thought, in a dispatch from Tunis describing the meeting of the United States second corps with troops of the British eighth army in the course of the fighting there. I quote from the dispatch:
Lieutenant Alvin J. Parker, of Odessa, Texas, who was in charge of a reconnaissance party at the junction, expressed the sentiments of the Americans when he said, "We ivere damned glad to see the British. They have done a great job. We have a lot to learn, but we are finding out how to take care of ourselves."
The last words are the important part. The units of our Canadian army should be given an opportunity to find out how to take care of themselves in the midst of battle. Consequently, if battle experience is advisable for the units of the Canadian army, why have they not had it? Why do they not get it?
Some believe that Canadian government policy has been to insist on holding the whole army together, to insist on keeping it

War Appropriation-Army
from fighting until it can fight as an army. Some believe that that has been the policy of the Canadian commanders overseas. Now, in his statement to the committee, the minister says that such is not the case. He says that the government has offered to allow units to be detached; that the Canadian commanders overseas have offered to allow units to be detached, but that the British government has not accepted, that the British government has said it did not want that done. That may or may not be accurate, but to me it sounds a great deal like placing the blame in a very subtle manner at the door of the British, which has been done by this ministry on more than one occasion since the outbreak of the war. If battle experience is desirable for our Canadian divisions and troops before the Canadians fight as an army, it is the duty of the Canadian government-it is not a matter to be left necessarily to the British-to see to it that our units get that battle experience before the Canadian army goes into action as an army. The government of the day cannot evade the responsibility for seeing that our boys get the proper amount of battle experience. So much for our army overseas.
I should now like to draw the attention of hon. members to the human side of the Canadian army. The minister has not said one word about that, in the course of his long statement.
In Canada vre regard our men as individuals. We look upon our troops, not as cogs in a machine, not as cannon-fodder, but as individuals. When Canadians in general think of the army they think of their sons, their husbands, their brothers or their friends. It is a personal matter; the human side of the army appeals to us. And I suggest it is the duty and the responsibility of the defence department of Canada to find ways of helping the men in the forces. But the defence department seldom show any signs of recognizing that responsibility: they leave it to some other department, such as the Department of Pensions and National Health. I propose this evening to give several examples.	.
First of all, there is this practice of discharging men as unfit too quickly. Some provision should be made so that such men will not be discharged until it is known whether they are to get a pension. There is too much of this business of throwing men out of the army as soon as they are able to walk away from the hospital and leaving them to worry for months as to whether they are to get any pension.
In the same connection, the defence department should insist on a change in our pen-

sion law, so that men disabled in the service will be able to get a pension. In very many cases men go into the army as category A and are discharged later as category E, yet they are unable to get a pension. One of the reasons is that our pension law is such that if a man has not served outside Canada, he can get a pension only if he shows -I quote from section 11, subsection 2 of the Pension Act-that-
.	.	. the injury or disease or aggravation
thereof resulting in disability or death . . . arose out of or was directly connected with such military service.
In other words, he must show that his disability arose directly out of something he was doing as a soldier. That was not the law in the last war, and it was not the law in this war, in Canada, up to May 21, 1940. Since then, it has been the law with regard to men serving in the army in Canada. It is far too rigid. It should be changed, and it is the responsibility of the defence department to see that some change is made.
It is true that provision is made for hardship cases. Where there has been serious disability, and the applicant is in necessitous circumstances, the pension commission may in its discretion award such amount as it deems adequate. But that is not wide enough to cover the cases of many of these men; many have gone in as category A, and have come out as category E, and yet cannot get a pension. Everyone knows that in many cases it is only too obvious that these men would not have been category E if they had not been in the army, although the disability may not have arisen out of anything they did directly as soldiers. I say, that has hurt enlistments across Canada for many months, and the act should be changed.
Another provision that should be made for the troops is this. Something should be done about helping their dependents to get homes. They should be able to get into wartime houses, and they should be able to take advantage of the National Housing Act; the Department of National Defence has a responsibility to take some interest in getting this consideration for the men.
A few months ago there was an increase in pay, but now we find that there are jokers in this increase. The idea got abroad in Canada that if a man served for so many months he would get an increase in pay, but now we find that there are provisos. He must be efficient, his conduct must have been good, and of course the test of that depends in many cases on the whim of his commanding
War Appropriation-Army

officer. There are too many penalties attached to the increase in pay. The provisions are not fair to the men in the forces.
Again, some provision should be made for protecting the insurance of men who join the forces. A man joins up and does not receive enough pay to pay his premiums, and some provision should be made to safeguard him against the cancellation of his policy.
These are a few of the points that should be of interest to the department. I think the situation may be summed up by saying that the men and women in the armed forces are making great sacrifices for Canada and that they and their dependents must be so treated, both during service and thereafter, that they will be adequately compensated for such sacrifices; and the responsibility rests upon the Department of National Defence to see that this is done.
The third subject which I wish to place before the committee this evening is this. The minister has made no declaration concerning the government's policy in the Pacific, in the war with Japan. He referred to two theatres of war, the European and the North American, if you please. I would remind him that there is also a Pacific theatre and that Canada is vitally concerned in that theatre. We may wake up one of these mornings to find that the Japanese have attacked our west coast. We may find that we have a war of our own right on our own front door-step. The minister said that Germany was the backbone of the axis. There can be no doubt that Germany is one of the backbones of the axis, but I suggest that there are two backbones, the other being Japan. She is a great distance away and is very hard to get at. She has a great navy, which is not the case w'ith Germany. She has a great army; her troops are filled with fanaticism, to a far greater degree than the German troops, and she has all the resources she needs, thanks to the conquests she has made in this war. In our war with Japan there is no Russia fighting on our side, and doing most of the fighting, as Russia has done against Germany.
Japan went into this war knowing exactly what she was doing and exactly what she wanted, and she went in with one aim, namely, world domination. Canada must never forget the deadly menace of Japan; yet apparently the government's policy is that Canada should turn her back on the Pacific war and fight a defensive war in that theatre; that Canada should fight what we may describe as a holding war. Well, at the moment Japan is doing all the holding in the Pacific. She has done the conquering, and now she is doing the holding and is being given time to consolidate her gains, with very few exceptions.

The actions of the Department of National Defence are in line with this policy of fighting a holding war in the Pacific. Canada's Pacific army has been stripped of general service personnel. They have been replaced by home defence personnel who cannot be sent abroad. Further than that, men sent to the units have not been men from the district or even the province to which these units belong. Men have been sent into units helter-skelter from all over Canada, which makes a complete hodge-podge. Hon. members can imagine what effect that has on the esprit de corps of a unit. No troops, so far as we know, have been sent to Australia, even for battle training against the Japanese, let alone being sent there as a token force to help the Australians and to show that Canada is beside them. The United States could send troops to Australia, but Canada, so far as I know, has not sent a man. The whole training of the Pacific army has been for defensive fighting, and I suggest to the minister that you cannot build a real fighting machine if it is for home defence only. One result of this defensive role is that many demands are made that the men from that Pacific army be taken away and put into logging, into the mining industry and into farming. The argument is used that they are only there for defensive purposes and that they should be put into these other industries instead of being kept in the army. That is the position and it is not a good one. Canada in the Pacific is leaving it to Australia, New Zealand, the United States, the Netherlands, China and Great Britain to fight the Japs, although we are a nation on the Pacific.
Perhaps Canada is not expecting to fight Japan at all unless it be on the shores of Canada, or it may be that the government expects men from the Canadian army overseas to fight Japan after they have finished fighting Germany. I suggest that the Canadian government should give a definite assurance to the other nations I have mentioned that Canada will fight in the Pacific beside those nations until Japan is conquered. Great Britain gave the United States that assurance a few weeks ago, but Canada has not done so.
I suggest further that we should prepare our Pacific army for offensive action; that we should make it available for service anywhere, just as the United States has done. American troops on the Pacific are available to fight wherever they are sent. I suggest that we send some units to Australia for battle experience; or, if the government will not do that, let them send at least some men from the various units. If this change were made; if the offensive spirit were instilled into the army, it would change the whole outlook on

the Pacific coast. I suggest that Canada should take her place in the offensive against the Japanese wherever they can be found, and that we should join with Australia, New Zealand and China in complaining about the indifference to the Pacific war.
