But they should be made available for service wherever they are required, in whatever theatre of war they may be needed. We shall require fewer men called up if those secured under the National Resources Mobilization Act are made available for service overseas. Therefore it will bring about economy in man-power. It will help to equalize sacrifice. It will get us away from the position where half the army will fight and the other half may not have to fight. The present man-power plan is not and never has been one to help win this war, but it has been a plan to win votes. Oh, I did not expect the ministers to like that. The Canadian people know this; they have no faith in the manpower policy for the army. I point out to the ministry-and if they are not interested, as perhaps they are not, then I point out to the members of this house-that the time has come to change this plan, and the lead should come from the Minister of National Defence. This afternoon he pleaded fervently for the Canadian people to have the conviction that men should go into the army, the navy and the air force. I suggest that before making that plea he should put his own house in order on this question of man-power.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say .a brief word about what I consider the most important part of the armed services, namely, the chaplain service. By some this might not be considered as having first place; but the equipment of a soldier, is he is to be a real soldier, is that which is imparted to him through the chaplain service, and begun in the home. Any agency which stimulates a man's faith in God does the best possible service for that man. Through it the man must have in him the belief that he can never die because, as the young soldier has said, "The cause is bigger than I am,"
When some of these young fellows get away from home they forget what they have been taught. They slip, and they do the things for which they condemn themselves in their 
own eyes. Then comes the army chaplain who shows how that young soldier can be forgiven. He sets the soldier on his feet again, so that he can go out and do his duty. These chaplains are not sissies. I know many of them who were athletes of the first water, men who did not carry their hearts on their sleeves, but who were not afraid of the faith and belief they had in them, which they practised every day. If the young man in the army feels that through his chaplain-I care not whether he be Protestant, Roman Catholic or Jewish-there is a means through which he can be forgiven, and made fit, then that chaplain is doing something to make the young man a first class soldier.
There is, in my opinion, no service rendered by any agency, in equipping soldiers, which compares with the chaplain service. A Frenchman once said to an Englishman, "When do you hope to retake Calais?" The Englishman replied, very intelligently, "When your sins become greater than ours". That is one of the things we hold up to our young men to-day, and one of the reasons why we lend our money in victory loan campaigns. That is one of the reasons why our young men are offering their lives. They believe that we are right, and that we are going to win out in the end.
I pay this tribute, as intelligently as I can in this hurried fashion, to the outstanding service rendered by the chaplains in all branches of the services.

Mr. Chairman, the minister this afternoon gave a very long and comprehensive statement respecting his department. I have a great deal of feeling for the position in which he finds himself. Owing to the fact that we have been secure from attack; that the Canadian forces have not been in action to any great extent-with the exception of one operation-and that there have been no extensive casualty lists, it is inevitable that the urgency of obtaining men for the army, the tremendous need for raising and equipping that army, and having it ready, is not as close to the minds of many people in Canada as might otherwise be the situation.
I agree with the minister when he says there is a tendency, every time man-power is required, to look to the army as the source from which it should come. I for one support the minister when he says that this tendency ought not to be allowed to continue, and that this war in the final analysis will have to be won by an invasion of enemy territory, through the use of a powerful, striking land force. If that is to be done, these men will have to be

War Appropriation-Army
raised, trained, equipped and ready. It is not a game which can be played in an in-again, out-again, on-again fashion.
I am sure all who are connected with the reserve army will be pleased with, the commendation he expressed this afternoon. As one who plays a very humble part in that army, I would say that in the last year it has taken a new lease on life. There seems to be a new grip, or a new sense of reality in the work it is doing. That is so at least in. the limited field in which I have had experience.
It has better equipment, and the men feel that they are now doing a really worth-while ^ job. However, there are things to be done yet. In many places they have difficulty in obtaining training equipment and suitable accommodation. That, of course, may be on account of local conditions. In the main, however, I have found a much better esprit de corps among the men of the reserve army, and the feeling that they are being permitted to fill a very useful role in Canada's war-time effort.
I believe an excellent job has been done in connection with cadets. At first there was a tendency to lay all the emphasis on air-force cadets, and as a result of the romance which comes of an age which belongs to the air, the army cadets had a tendency to fall behind. Emphasis is now being properly placed on army cadets, and a greater number of young high-school boys are being directed to army cadet units. I believe a real service can be rendered in that respect. A number of boys have written me asking my opinion about joining cadet units. I have replied in every case that, having served in those units, when the time comes for their entrance into the army they will make better soldiers, after having taken advantage of that preliminary training. I have pointed out that they will be better able physically and mentally to render the best possible service as a soldier.
May I now say a word about something the minister discussed a few days ago. It had not been my intention to say anything more about the Dieppe operation. I asked a question with respect to it on February 15, and on Friday last the minister gave me his rather belated answer. At that time he enunciated, in my opinion, a strange doctrine of responsible government. As reported at the top of page 2689 of Hansard, he said:
I do not believe, and I do not think the committee believes-I am of opinion that the country will agree with me in this-that to give our military leaders the impression that every time they plan an operation they must bear in mind that they will have to justify every detail
of that action before a tribunal of civilian strategists in Ottawa or elsewhere, is a good thing.
That seems to me to be a new doctrine of responsible government. I confess to being a civilian, and make no apology for it; it is not my fault that I am. I make no claim to being a strategist, and least of all a military strategist. But I do say to the minister that so long as I sit in this chamber-and I believe I can speak for my colleagues-I intend to hold the minister responsible, and I expect him to hold his senior officers responsible., and them in turn to hold responsible their subordinate officers, for every life that is lost by virtue of negligence, carelessness or stupidity. I have no objection to the men who are planning the operations having to keep in mind that they will be held responsible for what they do; that they in turn will be held responsible by their superior officers; that those superior officers will be held responsible by the general staff; that the general staff will be held responsible by ' the minister, and that in turn the minister will feel he is being held responsible by the House of Commons. If that is not to be done, then we have not responsible government, and we shall have merely a military dictatorship.
I suggest that the hon. member read the passage again, and see if he has not set up a straw man so as to knock it down.

I would refer to the statement which the minister made and in which he quoted General Marshall as follows:
. . . individuals with only a superficial knowledge of military matters or of the actual facts in the particular case. I submit that there is a clear line of demarcation between the democratic freedom of discussion, which we are determined to preserve, and a destructive procedure which promotes discontent and destroys confidence in the army.
I wish to say to the minister that I am not one of those persons who have indulged in the throwing of brickbats at brass hats. That is very often a cheap form of entertainment. Neither am I one of those who think that brass hats are infallible. There are veterans of the last war who will tell us, and the history books bear them out, something of the story of Passchendaele and other great blunders that were made by some of the military leaders. In our own day and generation most people have not forgotten Singapore and Tobruk, and the leaders of the general staff in Great Britain who said in 1940 that Hitler had missed the bus.
War Appropriation-Army
Does the hon. member not think Hitler did miss the bus?
H he missed the bus., he certainly caught something much faster when one considers the way in which he moved around for the six weeks following the time that statement was made.
He is missing the bus pretty badly right now.

I suggest that one of the functions of democratic government is the responsibility which we in this house have to ask questions, to query certain things which are done. In connection with the Dieppe operation I would refer the committee to some questions which were asked at Westminster and which are reported at page 767 of the British Hansard of September 30, 1942. I quote:
Mr. Henderson Stewart asked the Prime Minister whether he has now been able to consider the full reports from the service departments on the Dieppe raid and in particular, upon the support afforded by the Royal Air Force to the army; whether he is satisfied that that support was adequate and effective; and whether any further measures are to be taken to meet the demands of the army for still closer support from the air arm m future actions?
The Prime Minister: During the course of the operation the military force commander made a signal which included the statement that air support was "faultless". The answer to the second part of the question is "yes." As regards the third part of the question, the problem of air support for the army is under constant examination.
Mr. Shinwell: Has the right hon. gentleman any information regarding the performance of the tanks that were landed, and is the report encouraging?
The Prime Minister: I have not in my mind at present any special information on the subject. I understand that they were held up by the altogether unexpected strength of blocks at the ends of the streets, which it had not been anticipated they would not be able to destroy by the fire of their guns. I have not any other particular item in my mind on the subject. They were. I believe, Churchill tanks, which no doubt explains the friendly interest in their performances, but I have not heard that they acquitted themselves with any marked lack of propriety.
. Mr. Shinwell: Will the right hon. gentleman give some attention to the matter of the gun mountings of these Churchill tanks that were used in the Dieppe raid?
The Prime Minister: They are under the most continuous study, change and improvement. A very large number in this country are being tested in every way, hut the point that the "?n* gentleman has made will, I am sure, attract the attention of the service departments concerned.
Then follows a series of questions with reference to casualties and certain equipment. 
I cite these to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that these men who were civilian strategists had a responsibility to discharge. In a democratic form of government we do not necessarily expect that every person who asks the minister a question must be an authority on military affairs. I noticed that when I asked the minister some questions the Ottawa Citizen did me the great honour of printing a long editorial which made the sarcastic suggestion that it was too bad the general staff had not sent for me to help them plan the operation for the invasion of Dieppe. I have long passed the place where either [DOT] bullying or ridicule will frighten me away from something which I deem to be my duty.
I do not propose to refrain from asking questions simply because I cannot pose as an expert in a particular field. As a matter of fact, I would imagine that the Ottawa Citizen would not want to carry that principle too far. If that were true, one could not discuss currency and credit in this house unless one had been [DOT]a banker. I am certain the Ottawa Citizen would not agree with that. Nor could one do what the Minister of National Defence did when he led the attack on the wheat board act' unless one had grown wheat. The Minister of National Defence was quite an authority on wheat in this house, although on the prairies they used to say that they did not think he knew the difference between May wheat and Mae West.
In asking these questions-I shall deal with them more fully in a moment-I did not do so for the sake of embarrassing the government, but because I had had contact with men who came back from Dieppe. A unit raised in my own constituency, the South Saskatchewan Regiment, took a prominent and gallant part in that operation. I have talked to men who have seen some of the confidential reports of the operation, and I felt it was only right and proper that these questions should be asked.
I would draw the attention of the committee to the opinion, not of a civilian strategist with only superficial information, as the minister says, but of certain people who are authorities. For instance, I draw attention to an article written by Henry Peterson, who has become one of the best known writers on military affairs at the present time. This appeared in Saturday Night of October 17, and reads as follows:
And if Dieppe was an army show, army intelligence should have been able to discover, in a friendly city-Dieppe is not a German city -the weight of the tank traps set up against invasion, without having to test them with 6-pounder guns, at the price of heaven knows how many lives.

War Appropriation-Army
And again:
For more than two years we have been saying that if our land forces only had proper air protection, proper equipment and proper training they would make short work of the enemy. Well, wre had all three at Dieppe, and Dieppe was a severe failure, for the losses far outweighed the gains by any measure that is not corrupted by wishful thinking. What, then, was wrong? There is only one factor left, a factor which we must put in a foremost place in our thinking if we are ever to learn this business of war; and that factor was generalship.
And again:
Does not the Dieppe affair smack most distressingly of Passchendaele-a four-square plan worked out "scientifically" and then launched without regard to what might happen between the sailing of the invasion ships and their arrival on the enemy coast?
And again:
. . . but still the four-square plan was pushed through, irrespective of the changed circumstance. . . . Surely this is to trust to heaven knows what, but certainly not to brains.
I would refer to another gentleman who can hardly be classified as a civilian strategist with only superficial knowledge, the Admiral of the Fleet, Lord Keyes, who formerly was in charge of combined operations and who is probably one of the best authorities in the world on amphibian warfare. Lord Keyes, speaking at Cambridge, England, on March 10-I shall not read all his statement because some of it has to do with British matters and has no point in our discussion-had this to say:
"As events proved the main landing at Dieppe against a heavily defended position did not take place early enough to secure the beach and permit the tanks which were timed to land after daylight to make good their landing," Lord Keyes said.
"They were all knocked out by well-sited anti-tank guns which could not be dealt with either from the air or the sea."
He conceded that the fact that more than 300 vessels crossed the channel through a minefield which had to be swept and that with the exception of one, that carrying the third commando, they arrived at their destinations at the appointed times was "greatly to the credit of the navy."
But, he said, it was never explained why this convoy was not reported to the naval officer in command in time to have it intercepted and dealt with before it could report the presence of a large force of troops, approaching the coast, as it evidently did with disastrous results.
Lord Keyes criticized the "pernicious system" of inter-service committees which he charged had frustrated British initiative and daring in this war.
"It is humiliating to us sailors that it should have been left to the Russians, Germans and Japanese to show us the way to wage an amphibious form of warfare, a form of warfare in which I am positive we could excel if only our high command could be induced to face some risks to win a great prize."
I refer to another who could hardly be classified as having superficial knowledge, Wallace Reyburn, who has written a book on Dieppe under the title, "Dress Rehearsal for Invasion." He of course landed with the troops at Dieppe. This is a report from London, dated April 8:
Wallace Reyburn, correspondent of the Montreal Standard, wrote to-day in a book, "Rehearsal for Invasion", based on his trip to Dieppe with the Canadian forces last August 19, that many lives were lost because invasion barges were not fitted with ropes by which troops in the water could climb aboard.
Reyburn said he himself was one man who did not have the strength to clamber up the flat side of a barge, rising four or five feet above the waterline, while under constant machinegun fire. The man next to him was shot and killed.
"The time wasted while men struggled to get into the landing craft at Dieppe cost many lives, and unnecessarily," Reyburn said.
"Most ships in the navy carry lengths of wide-mesh rope netting which are suspended out on a beam over the water when they are picking up men from the sea.
"It would have been a simple matter to have this type of rope netting suspended from each side of the landing craft and it would have been no trick at all for men to have climbed up it."
I refer to one more item reported from London, April 19, which states:
Hannen Swaffer, veteran London journalist, writing in The People, a Sunday paper with a circulation of more than 300,000, said Major-General J. H. Roberts, leader of last August's Dieppe raid, who recently was promoted to command all Canadian reinforcements overseas, has "been kicked upstairs."
He goes on to say that the transfer of the Canadian commander has added to the bewilderment,. That is the statement of Hannen Swaffer, a correspondent writing from Great Britain. He refers to the promotion of General Roberts as kicking him upstairs. The general feeling, he said, would be that people would be bewildered to understand why a man who had carried out operations supposed to have been successful should be retired to the training of reinforcements.
Is he a newspaper correspondent or a military man?
He is a newspaper correspondent, but a man who has some reputation as a military correspondent.
What is his name?
I have already given his name-Hannen Swaffer.
A correspondent for the News of the World, I think.

He writes in a paper called The People.

War Appropriation-Army
It is the same sort of paper.

There is some other evidence that cannot be discarded as being superficial. I refer to the photographs that were dropped over England by German planes. These photographs do not show a particularly pleasant picture. They show pretty clearly large numbers of tanks immobilized on the beach at Dieppe and some submerged in the water. I notice in the Montreal Standard, of May 8, an article by Wallace Reyburn which states that the newspapers correspondents have just been shown a German film which was being sent to South America and was intercepted by the British, and the picture was shown to the newspaper correspondents and was not a very pleasant picture to see. Naturally, of course, the picture was touched up to suit German propaganda purposes. It gives the impression that the Canadian troops did not even get into Dieppe, which Reyburn says is not correct. He says that most of the newspaper men came away from seeing that picture rather grim and depressed. As a matter of fact, I would suggest to the minister that if that picture could be secured, it might be a good idea to show it to the newspaper men and the members of the house, and it might be a suitable film for study by officers planning tactics with a view to invasion.
I come now to the four questions which I asked the minister. The minister prefaced his answers by saying that he was not going to answer any more questions. He might just as well have not answered at all, if I may say so without giving offence, because 'his answer was so delightfully vague and beautifully evasive that it served no purpose at all.
My first question to the minister was why there had been no preparatory aerial bombardment. The minister answered that question by asking some questions. He said:
Does this committee for a moment suppose that in the careful planning and preparation for this operation that question was not discussed by the military planners?
Then he answers his own question:
I do not think so.
Then he says:
I cannot give the committee the reasons for the changes that occurred.
Well, Colonel Fraser, who came back, gave reasons. He said that the reason was that it was felt that aerial bombardment would cause so much debris and rubble on the streets as to make it difficult for the tanks to operate. If that is the reason, the minister might have

told us that. If that is not the reason, Colonel Fraser ought not to have been making statements of that kind to the public.
But the strangest thing of all is that the minister answers the question by saying this:
Let me ask: is there anyone in this committee who would say that those officers were wrong? Is there anyone in this committee who would say that the results of the operation would have been different had a different plan been followed?
Well, is there anyone who would say that the results would not have been different? It is just as easy to answer the question one way or the other. What we do know is that the operation was not an unqualified success, and for the minister to say that we do not know that the results would have been different even if there had been an aerial bombardment does not answer	the	question,	because	there isequally the	possibility that	the results	might
have been different had the invasion been preceded by aerial bombardment.

My hon. friend wants to be fair, I think, but he has left out the most important part of what I said in that connection. I	said	that the	matter	of	aerial
bombardment had been the subject of consideration by senior Canadian and British officers and that they had decided on the plan after the changes were made. That is the part my hon. friend has not read. It seems to me that that is the most important part of the answer to his question. What I said was this:
I cannot give the committee the reasons for the changes	that	occurred.	To do	so	would
mean that I must recall senior officers from England to give a full account of deliberations and discussions that covered weeks of time, and the result would be that we would disclose our whole hand to the enemy. But senior Canadian and British officers agreed on the final plan after the most thorough and exhaustive deliberation of the matter, and aerial bombardment was one of the features which were the subject of discussion.
It seems to me that one does not have to go very much further than that unless my hon. friend has some ground for questioning the judgment and the ability of the officers who made that decision.

Nothing but political
grounds.

That, of course, is just the cheap sort of remark which we expect from the hon. member for Parry Sound. I will not give serious consideration to it at the present moment.
I do not think the minister's point alters the case I am presenting. The minister said

War Appropriation-Army
that it was given serious consideration, but he cannot give the grounds. I am not pressing him to give the grounds; I am merely pointing out. why he could not give the grounds. Colonel Fraser, who came back, did give as a reason-

Unfortunately I was not
there as Colonel Fraser was, but I did see the report of the committee, and I stated I could not give the reasons. I said, however, that changes were made, and were made by a committee of extremely responsible and senior officers, not only Canadian but British. I mentioned some of them in another part of my report.
I know. I merely point out that that does not answer the question.

I would think it would,
for most people.

Then that should have been the end of the answer, instead of going on to ask hypothetical questions as to whether it would make any difference one way or the other.
The next question was as to landing at high tide or low tide. Again the minister indulges in a rhetorical observation, that he does not think the committee can conceive of officers planning such an operation and not taking such matters into account. The fact is, whether they took them into account or not, that that was the actual situation; these men did land at high tide and were taken off at low tide, when they had to cross some four hundred yards of open beach under heavy machine-gun fire.
Is my hon. friend prepared to express the opinion that they would have been safer to stay on the beach an hour or two more until the tide came up, under fire such as he has described?

If the minister will let me finish, I will say what I intended to say. At the bottom of the column I find this statement:
The decision to withdraw the troops was a military decision, taken at a time when our men were actually engaged in combat with a determined enemy.
If the point the minister is making now is that it was a matter of taking them off rather than at a later time; that it was a military decision dictated by the exigencies of the moment, that is one argument. But when the Dieppe operation was first being publicized in the newspapers the statement was made that these men were taken off within six
72537-177 J
minutes of the actual time that had been set out in the plan for the operation prior to leaving England. That does not jibe with the minister's statement. If these men were taken off within six minutes of the actual time set out in the plan of operations, it must have been planned to take them off at low tide. That is a very different thing from having to take them off on account of any given military situation.
It is a different situation altogether. There was fire on the beach. Are you going to leave them there?
They were not on the beach at the time they were withdrawn. They were brought from the town and across the beach.
The operation was supposed to be over.
The minister is not going to twist me out of the point.

I have my hon. friend's point exactly. I have not looked at the plan, and I have not in mind the exact hour for withdrawal: I do not know that I have seen it. The exact hour for withdrawal might have been eleven o'clock, and that would have been perfectly all right, but that hour for withdrawal was no doubt based on the fact that the operation was complete and that the troops had made their circle of the town and come back. The withdrawal which was made, however, was in the face of heavy fire; and my hon. friend is suggesting that they should have stayed on the beach for an hour or two longer until the tide came in.

The minister knows I am not making any such suggestion. He is a clever courtroom lawyer, but he is not going to make me say something I did not say. I at no time suggested that they should stay on the beach.
Where would they go?
I say that if this statement is correct, that these men were taken off within six minutes of the time that it was planned to take them off, and that was when the tide was out-
Who made that statement?
That statement was made at the time that the operation was being lauded in the press right across Canada.
By whom?

I think we are entitled to an answer to that question.
War Appropriation-Army

The minister is not entitled to anything. I did not ask him to interrupt me. I have the floor, and I do not propose to have the Minister of Mines and Resources bobbing up and down. I do not mind the Minister of National Defence bobbing up and down. But one is enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think it is within the discretion of the hon. member who has the floor whether he will answer questions asked of him.

My third question was with reference to the breaching of the sea wall; and again, the minister says that this task had been assigned to engineers and they were unable under the circumstances to breach the sea wall. The minister then says that some tanks did manage to get into the town. I asked the minister, how many? He would not say how many. My information was that it was one tank. The minister says it was more than one. I see now that, according to "Combined Operations", a booklet which has been printed by the British war office, three tanks managed to get by the tank blocks which had been put at the end of the street, by breaking through some houses, and made their way into the town of Dieppe.

My hon. friend's statement is:
What astounds me is not that none of the tanks got off the beach but that those who planned the operation ever expected them to.

That is right; and at that time my information was that none of them did get off. Since that time the statement has been made in "Combined Operations" that three of them got off. The minister knows that this was three out of a very large number; I do not know that it is wise to state how many there were, but there were many times three, as the minister knows. *The three that did get into the town were not able to effect the objective. The statement I made then is borne out by the minister's own statement that the engineers were unable to breach the wall- that the inability to breach the wall, plus the fact that, as Mr. Churchill said in the statement I just read, the tank blocks at the end of the streets were much heavier than they expected, because they thought they could blast them with their 6-inch guns and found that they could not, made it impossible for those tanks to get in.
While I was wrong in saying that none got off. that was my information at the time. Three getting off is not very many tanks to succeed in the tactical objective which had been set by those outlining the plan. The fact remains that the failure to breach the sea wall
and the failure to remove these tank obstacles constituted one of the contributing factors in the inability to crown the operation with complete success.
And to what does my hon. friend attribute that?
I beg the minister's pardon?
The failure to breach the wall and to remove the obstacles; to what does my hon. friend attribute that?

I would say that one of the things is that one would have thought the intelligence service would have been able to give the necessary information as to the location of such prominent tank traps as blocks of concrete at the ends of the streets. The same would be true as regards the sea wall-a twelve-foot sea wall. While the minister says that there are places where the sea wall dipped-I have walked along it, although not recently, but probably it has not greatly changed-it is quite a formidable obstacle, even to infantry, let alone armoured fighting vehicles.
May I a^k the hon. member if he has ever taken part in a landing like this?

Has the
minister?
I have. That is just the difference.
I am sure everyone has heard about that. It is not necessary to advertise it.
The hon. member knows now, anyway.

The fourth question I was asking was with reference to the supply of small arms; and the minister said-and I am satisfied) with that statement -that the scale of supply was as generous as the means of transport and the conveying capacity of the men would) allow in operations of this kind. I believe that is correct. I should like the minister to have gone a little further, although, as reported at page 2688 of Hansard, he made a statement which I think will commend itself to the committee:
If there were lessons to be learned, they have been noted, and if there were things which might be considered as faults or defects those have been given particular attention.
I think that is the kind of spirit which this committee and the people of Canada will want, because it is only by actual experience
fMr. Crerar.]

War Appropriation-Army
that we can know what these men require and whether or not the equipment we have is suitable.
I do not know whether the minister has reports-I imagine he has-with reference, for instance, to the Sten gun. I suppose he has reports with reference to mortars. My information is that since the Dieppe operation the number of mortars per unit has been substantially increased, and I sincerely hope it has. All the information I was able to get from men who have been over there was that the efficient use of the mortar by the Germans was terrifying, and they are using a much heavier mortar with a very much longer range and much more effective technique than we have been able to master. The same will no doubt be true of the need for more anti-tank guns per unit. All I was asking the minister for, and I am glad to have his assurance, is that some of the lessons which have been learned from the performance of our weapons, as compared with the weapons which the enemy had, have taught those who are responsible such lessons as will enable' them to plan for the coming invasion on a scale that will make it possible for our men to meet the enemy on equal terms.
There are only one or two more observations which I wish to make with reference to this matter. Nothing has been said yet as to who was actually in command of the Dieppe operation. We do not know whether it was carried out under General McNaughton as commander of the Canadian forces overseas, or whether it was under Lord Mount-batten who was in charge of the combined operation. I do not know why this should have been left in doubt. Major-General Roberts was in charge of the Canadian troops, but who was in charge of the general operation? Who planned it? That is information which the people ought to have. We should know something also of the real purpose. The minister said that it was for information and experience. If that was the purpose, whether it was for battle experience or in order to sound out the enemy position and to ascertain their relative strength, we ought to know.
I am sure the minister will be prepared to give an assurance to the committee that as a result of the Dieppe operation everything necessary is being done to bring about the closest possible coordination of the different arms of the services. As Lord Keyes said, amphibious warfare is the most intricate of all kinds of warfare, and the closest possible liaison between the army, the navy and the
air force is necessary if an operation like this is to be a success. In view of the fact that an invasion of, the continent will involve operations much more complicated and on a gigantic scale, I am sure the minister will be glad to give the committee the assurance that the fullest possible coordination is taking place in training between the three services in preparation for the invasion.
Before leaving the Dieppe operation, I should like to make a suggestion to the minister with reference to some of the men who took part. I do not know who is responsible for giving awards or recommending them to his majesty, but a story came back from Dieppe which was printed in most of our papers about one of the padres who succeeded in getting to a barge when he found that some Canadians would have to be left behind. He left his barge, dived into the sea and went back to join the men on the beach.
I think that is one of the most gallant things, one of the finest examples of self-sacrifice that has come out of the war, and if it lies in the power of the minister I hope that some recognition will be given to that man, whoever he is. I do not know his name, but the chances are that the minister does.
This booklet on the combined operation, issued by the British war office, mentions some heroic Canadians, and I hope that consideration will1 be given to them. I refer particularly to Lieutenant Patterson of Canning-ton, Ontario, who managed to break through the tank obstacles at the end of the street. Then there are Private Sodden of Vancouver, Major MacTavish of Moose Jaw and Major David Orme of Weyburn. Both the latter showed, according to this booklet, outstanding gallantry in actually leaving their landing barges and going back to silence German machine-gun nests that were firing on the men who were being loaded into boats. These gallant officers did not return and are prisoners of war in Germany to-day. Talking to men who have come back, I find that some of them feel that they owe their lives to the courage and resourcefulness of these two officers, Macintosh and Orme, and there is a feeling that some recognition should be given to them for these outstanding feats of gallantry.
I wish to say just one or two more things before I sit down so as to avoid rising again when the committee proceeds. I cannot agree with those who, in the press and in the house, have been constantly urging the minister to have the Canadian army broken up and sent to various theatres of war. I noticed that the minister reiterated throughout his speech the
War Appropriation-Army

fact that the Canadian army had been kept together not by any wish of this government or its commander, but at the request of the British government. I do not think the minister needs to make any apology, even if his government is responsible, for keeping the Canadian, army as a unit. It is true there is a great deal of value in taking non-commissioned officers and officers and sending them to Africa or elsewhere to gain battle experience, but I think the great majority of the Canadian people-I cannot speak for the majority of Canadian soldiers, but certainly I can say the same of hundreds of them to whom I have spoken-feel that the Canadian army should be kept as a unit under its commander, and that when it goes into battle it should go in as a Canadian unit under a Canadian commander. I do not think the minister needs to apologize, nor do I think he needs to bow to the pressure of those who are suggesting that the army should be broken up and sent to various theatres of war.

The minister did not do
either.

The hon. member for Parry Sound can make his own statement. The minister is capable of stating what he did or did not say without the assistance of the hon. member for Parry Sound.
I would mention a matter discussed by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), namely, the question of pay. There was considerable elation when it was announced that pay was to be increased in the army, and it certainly was about time. But on account of provisos there have been some strange anomalies. For instance, there is the proviso that a man must have taken basic training. The other day I spoke to a young man who had been instructing. When he joined the army, as a result of previous experience he had had he was told that he did not need basic training, and accordingly he was sent to take a special course. After a while he was instructing. Under the new regulations he must be 6ent back to basic training, and there he finds other instructors who have been sergeants and sergeant-majors who are now also taking basic training in order to qualify for increased pay. That seems to me to be an anomalous situation, and I am sure it is something that has been overlooked. I direct it to the minister's attention. There is also the proviso that a man should have been an efficient soldier. That sounds excellent, but it leaves room for discrimination and makes it possible for an officer who has taken a dislike to a man to punish him by refusing to recommend him for this 
increased pay. I think there would be a better feeling all round if the increased pay came into effect automatically when a man had reached a certain period of service in the army. The minister has said that consideration is already being given to raising the pay of the Canadian Women's Army Corps and particularly the raising of their trades pay; also that consideration is being given to the matter of dependents' allowances for the women. In view of the fact that these matters are being considered, I need not take time to advocate them now.
I should like to make one statement with reference to reinforcements. I think some effort should be made to retain the identity of the units. I have in mind, for instance, the South Saskatchewan Regiment, in which naturally I am interested. After Dieppe they required some sixteen officers. The second battalion of the regiment supplied over forty reinforcement officers, if my memory serves me correctly; but not more than one, if any, of those officers went to the first battalion; they were sent to other battalions, while officers from other units were brought in to the South Saskatchewan Regiment. There is a value in having together men who come from a particular community, particularly when men come out as reinforcements. They have seen the boys' friends, their parents and their sweethearts; they bring news from home, and they have a community of interest. I think that is something worth while, something that helps build up morale. When men go from the second battalion to the reinforcement pool it seems to me that if at all possible those men should be forwarded to the first battalion, in the interests of efficiency and morale. They know the men with whom they are going to work, the men whom they are going to lead into action.
All I wrant to say in closing, Mr. Chairman, is that we in this corner realize that the minister has a difficult task. I should not like him to think that we propose to spend the time, while we are discussing the estimates of his department, in mere carping criticism. He has a tremendous task ahead of him. There have been a great many things come out of the training of the past few years, and particularly out of this Dieppe operation. There are two things the minister is not, in my opinion. He is neither complacent nor indolent, and I have confidence that the lessons which have been learned will be vigorously applied.
I express the wish and the hope that the minister will do everything possible to see that if there have been mistakes, if there have been weaknesses, if there have been defects, they will be remedied, because it will be our

War Appropriation-Army
responsibility in this house to hold him responsible, just as he must hold his senior officers responsible for the welfare and safety of every man under their command.

Before proceeding to discuss any of the points raised by the minister, I should like to refer to the matter mentioned by the hon. member for Fort William and the hon. member for Weyburn, who spoke in particular of certain men who had made heroic sacrifices at Dieppe, and went on to refer to the padre who jumped off the invasion barge and swam back in order to remain with his men on the beaches of Dieppe. The name of that young man is Captain Jack Foote, who was born and brought up in the village of Madoc, my home town. At the date of his enlistment he was in charge of the Presbyterian church at Port Hope, Ontario. His mother is at present residing in the city of Ottawa, where his sister holds a responsible position in the department of naval services. I might say further that only this week in speaking to the mother of this gallant young chaplain I was told that within the previous day or so she had received a letter from her son, who is now a prisoner of war in Germany. He stated that he was very glad he had jumped off the boat and swum back to remain with the boys, because he felt that in his position as padre he was able to do and was doing something worth while. This only bears out what was said by the hon. member for Fort William and the hon. member for Weyburn, that in this war the padres are doing a real job. I should like to join with the hon. member for Weyburn in drawing this gallant act to the attention of the minister, and I hope that in due time it will receive adequate recognition.
The minister stated that during the past year enlistments in the army had totalled some
125,000.	Would the minister be good enough to place on Hansard or to make available to the committee a break-down of these figures by military districts, at the same time showing the number of men called up during the past year in the military districts under the National Resources Mobilization Act?
Has that not been done? I know it was done up to December 31.
It has not been brought up to date. What I should like is the number who enlisted during the past year in each military district.
Has there not been a statement since December 31?
I have not the copy of "Canada at War" containing that statement, but I think it was the February issue.

I am speaking now of the document published, I think, by the war information board giving the figures up to December 31, showing the number enlisting and the number called up in each district. I have an idea that has been brought up to date; if not, that can be done.
I believe that shows the number who have enlisted and the number who have been called up from the beginning.
I think my hon. friend is right.

In connection with the 125,000 men the minister says enlisted during the last year, I am asking that he give a break-down by military districts, also showing the number called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act, by districts, because I think it would be very interesting to hon. members of the committee to know what part or parts of Canada are supplying a steady stream of recruits to the various branches of the armed forces. In reference to the number required for the present year, the minister stated that enlistments were down for March and April and that May had not started off any too well, but he did'not elaborate to any extent on the means by which he intended to raise the required number of men. It is quite true that in his remarks this afternoon he did make some reference to replacing men with older men and those in lower categories; to replacing men with women, and so on, but he did not go farther than that. Nor did he make any reference to the principle of compulsory selective military service for anywhere in the world.
I was disappointed that the minister did not make any reference to this very important matter. Surely, with the hour of the offensive drawing closer each day, the time is long past when we should allow this muddle in manpower to continue. I think this committee is entitled to know from the government, and especially from the Minister of National Defence, whether or not he is in favour of compulsory selective military service for members of the armed forces. As the hon. member for Vancouver South said, let us put an end to this farce of recruiting as it has existed up to date. The minister said this afternoon that to obtain recruits the department intended to carry on a vigorous course of recruiting.
When the minister makes a statement about compulsory selective military service, let him go a little further and say why the act has not been put into force. What is the reason? Is there some political reason behind it, or is there some fear on the part of the government that they will offend some section or
War Appropriation-Army

part of the dominion? Or is it just a continuation of the old; policy of isolation and appeasement? Surely it is only reasonable that if there are large numbers of trained men in Canada, those men should be available for service overseas, if they are required. When the minister replies he might state whether there is any truth in the rumour that at the present time regulations are being drafted under which home defence men will be available for service anywhere.
In regard to the training in Canada I would point out that the minister has made very little comment as to the types of such training. All hon. members remember the Hong Kong disaster, and the record of training up to that date. Perhaps when he speaks again the minister will explain the changes made, and how training in Canada has been improved since the time of the Hong Kong disaster.
In the March issue of the little booklet issued by the war information board, entitled "Canada at War", we find the following statement with respect to the army in Canada:
The training of troops is being brought to a completion as far as practicable in Canada, so that when they are sent abroad they will be prepared for actual combat.
I hope the minister will enlarge upon that statement, because I remember a previous statement made by him in which he explained that when the troops left Canada, upon arrival in England their qualifications and training were checked very carefully, and that they then embarked upon further intensive training.
. Would the minister also give the committee information as to the minimum training required in Canada before troops proceed overseas? I understand that the average course at basic training centres is about eight weeks, and that a further eight weeks is required for the advanced course. I have heard, however, that at some training centres it takes as long as twenty weeks or more to complete the eight weeks' course. I wish the minister to correct me if I am wrong, and state whether there is any truth in that report.
Would the hon. member name the centre?

I am told it is at Rimouski, Quebec.
_ Then, this afternoon the minister gave some information as to what had been done in respect of the training of parachute troops in Canada. However, he did not mention anything further about commando training, the training of a special service force or training in mountain warfare, nor did he say anything about what is contemplated with regard to the training of air-borne troops in Canada. Surely that type of training is ideally suited 
to Canada, in comparison with England. Then, would the minister give the committee information as to whether gliders are being used in Canada, or whether it is expected that glider troops will be trained.
During the debate last year on a similar measure the minister was good enough to place on Hansard a syllabus showing the types of training carried on in the various training centres, for the various branches. Would he be good enough to place a similar syllabus on Hansard this year to indicate the changes, and the advancements, if any, which have been made? At the same time would he include a record of the number of rounds fired by individual troops.
The minister stated there were some 190,000 troops overseas, and about 250,000 in Canada, which number would be reduced by some
15,000.	But will the minister go further and tell the committee why it is necessary to have 250,000 or even 235,000 troops in Canada? Surely he must know that the Canadian army overseas will certainly be in action long before the troops in Canada.
Did my hon. friend hear what I had to say about that? I made an explanation.
Yes; and of that 235,000 a very large number are fully trained troops, ready to go overseas.

Did my hon. friend hear what I said respecting the uses to which the Canadian army was put? I pointed out that a certain proportion were for home war establishment, a certain proportion for operational troops, and a certain number in training centres. What does my hon. friend suggest cutting down?
I do not think the minister broke down the figure, or said how many were to be kept for the defence of the east and west coasts.

Yes. I referred to the
operational troops. I said that 80,000 were operational troops, and I gave the posts, including Newfoundland, Labrador, Jamaica and Alaska. I gave the number of posts, and the number of areas to be defended. My hon. friend now asks me to give this information, but I have already given it once. I am interested to know what my hon. friend's comments will be, or if he has any suggestions as to where reductions might be made. I would welcome any such suggestions.

According to what the minister says, if he breaks that 250,000 into three parts, and keeps 80,000 for a home defence force, he will still have 160,000 for overseas.
I would point out that about 55,000 of another 80,000 are general service men in training centres, to go overseas, and the other 80,000 are in home war establishments.
When the minister refers to home war establishments does he refer to troops called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act?
I refer to everything. I am afraid my hon. friend did not pay me the compliment of listening to or reading what I said.
I listened to it, and read it.

Then my hon. friend did not get very far in understanding it. I said that of the 80.000, right off the bat about 32,000 were administrative and training staffs in the eighty-seven training centres, and that that left about 50,000. The veterans' guard came next.
