Something has already been said by two hon. members respecting pay, and comment was made by the minister. I would pass on to him an argument which has often been used with regard to the members of the women's army who are taking the places of men. It must be admitted that in many instances they are doing just as good and perhaps better work than the men wTere doing. In such cases it is urged that the women should receive at least 81.30 a day, or perhaps the 81.50 received by the men. I was pleased to hear the minister say that members of the women's corps would receive the same trade pay as is given to the men.
A point which has been raised in connection with earlier legislation of this kind has to do with the $20 a month paid to a mother, as compared with the S35 paid a wife. I have not heard any explanation from the department or the minister as to why the allowance for a mother was placed at $15 lower than that paid to a wife. I trust the minister will give us the yardstick or whatever means were used to arrive at the rates of these allowances.
When the minister speaks again, will he state whether any consideration has been given to increasing the rehabilitation grant to men
who have been discharged? At the present time it is only one month's pay. Speaking on a previous occasion in the house, I mentioned various safeguards that should be used in connection with property and insurance of members of the armed forces, and I should like to know if anything is contemplated to protect soldiers' property from being seized under distress warrants for taxes, mortgage .payments or anything of that kind. While I realize that these things come under the various provinces, perhaps the minister will tell the committee whether anything is being worked out in this connection. I should like the minister to give the committee at the proper time information as to the number of men who have been discharged from the armed forces and the number of those who are in receipt of pensions at the present time.
I wish to deal rather briefly with the question of Dieppe which has been referred to by other speakers to-night. I read very carefully the remarks of the minister, especially that part where he said that he hoped there would be no further discussion on this matter.

I did not hope that at all. I could not possibly hope that, knowing my hon. friend. What I did say was that I could not undertake or hope to answer all questions with regard to Dieppe, particularly those which would require my getting details from officers overseas or those who were busy on other matters.

The minister has dealt quite extensively with the Dieppe affair in the house, and he has made at least one speech outside the house. During the course of his remarks the hon. member for Weybum made reference to a certain editorial which stated that the Dieppe affair smacked of Passchendaele. There are many soldier members of this house who have most vivid recollections, some of them not very pleasant, of the ghastly mistakes and blunders that were made in the last war. I recall one quite well myself which occurred in connection with my own unit, which was the 44th battalion of Winnipeg. On October 24, 1916, during the battle of the Somme, there were between 300 and 400 casualties suffered in that one unit as a result of a blunder by some of the higher-ups.
The minister has been asked on previous occasions if he would make a full statement on Dieppe during a secret session, but apparently he has decided that there will be no secret session or further report from him on the Dieppe affair. I would point out to the minister that during last session there was a
War Appropriation-Army

long debate on the Hong Kong expedition, during which the minister made a lengthy defence of his department, the officers concerned and all the rest of it. At the conclusion of that debate, or some time afterwards, the minister announced in the house, if I remember correctly, that there had been some twenty or more changes in the staff of his department, directly as a result of the Hong Kong affair. If I am wrong in the number, perhaps the minister will correct me.

I will correct my hon.
friend about the whole thing. I made no statement that there were twenty changes.

Were there not various
changes made in the minister's department as a result of the Hong Kong affair?

My hon. friend said I
made a statement, and I have no recollection of making a statement that twenty or any number of changes had been made as a result of the Hong Kong affair.
Do I understand the minister to say that there were no changes made in his department as a result of Hong Kong?

My hon. friend does not
understand anything of the kind.

I accept the minister's word,
and I will check on that. It is rather interesting in connection with the Dieppe operation to notice that only to-day, if it is safe again to mention the Globe and Mail-

The hon. member does
not mention much else.
The minister may find out that I do mention much else. Perhaps he is still smarting on account of some of the editorials in the Globe and Mail.

I would be raw if I
bothered with the editorials in the Globe and Mail.

Perhaps the minister reads only the flattering ones. The objectives of the Dieppe operation were set out as being, first, a six-inch battery to be put out of commission; second, a wireless station to be demolished; third, an ammunition dump to be blown up; fourth, to gain information and experience; fifth, to inflict casualties on the enemy; sixth, to get prisoners and, seventh, to terrorize the enemy. The first three objectives, the battery, the wireless station and the ammunition dump, surely could have been achieved by means of the air force. Three, four, five or six bombers could easily have destroyed those

three installations and would probably have caused a great deal of damage to the enemy with only a few casualties.
The minister dwelt at some length on the information obtained and the experience gained which were used in future operations, but he overlooked entirely the other side of the picture. He made no mention of what our enemies gained from this operation. We can only guess at the number of German casualties, but I do remember a dispatch in a New York paper which placed them in the neighbourhood of 500. I have no recollection of ever reading in the press or hearing any statement about the number of prisoners brought back. One- can only assume that the number was very small. This may have been as a result of the fact that many Canadian troops had to swim out to the invasion barges, and naturally it would be rather difficult to take their equipment or to bring back prisoners, if they had taken any.
I should like to refer briefly to what information and benefit the enemy obtained and gained from this raid. It is well known that the enemy obtained complete copies of the operation orders, and as a result of this hundreds and hundreds of Canadian prisoners are still shackled up to a very recent date. The Germans were given a splendid opportunity to observe our invasion tactics, and it is safe to assume that they have taken all necessary steps to protect themselves and to deal with similar tactics in the future. If our invasion tactics were good at Dieppe, we have told the Germans all about them. They have obtained copies of the operation orders instead of their being kept secret for large scale operations in the future. The element of surprise in future operations has been eliminated.
The Germans were presented with at least several of the latest type of Churchill tanks and were given an opportunity of examining the armour, the guns, the engine .and everything else about them. I believe I am correct when I say that all the tanks landed at Dieppe remained on the shore. In addition, large quantities of rifles, Bren guns, mortars, tommy guns, revolvers and other equipment were left with the Germans. Signal equipment was also left behind, and at least one or more of the latest type of invasion barges was left for the Germans, thus giving them an opportunity to examine it and find out its most vulnerable spots, so that they can decide how best to deal with such barges in future operations.

War Appropriation-Army
The minister said during the course of his remarks that the percentage of casualties suffered at Dieppe is not a proper yardstick by which to measure future casualties. Well, so far as the Canadian army is concerned, Dieppe was either a ghastly failure or a great success.

There is no middle
ground?

We will come to that. If it was a failure, it was unfortunate. If it was a success as claimed by the minister, I think it naturally follows that the casualties at Dieppe are a fair example of the casualties to be expected in the future in similar operations. It has been stated time and again over the	radio and	in	the	press	that theCanadians are to be the spearhead of the invasion of the continent. This attack when it comes must necessarily be over water, assisted 'by the navy; but unlike the Dieppe operation	which lasted	only	some	eight ornine hours, when there is a permanent invasion and	the troops	are to	stay,	not onlymust they make a landing in the face of fortified positions, but they must immediately fan out if they are to survive. Not only will there be	casualties	on	the	first	day, butcasualties on the second day, the third day, the fourth day and so on, as long as they stay there. Such landings would naturally bring on heavy counterattacks. They would be subject to intense shelling and to dive bomber attacks. It is only reasonable to expect that the enemy would throw every possible bit of his equipment against them in order to knock out the attack before the attackers could land and fan out. Naturally, with an attack over water as must take place in any invasion of the continent, the attacking forces cannot have the protection of an artillery barrage.	On the other hand, the
enemy will have his own artillery to use against the invaders. Any comparison of the number of prisoners lost by the Canadian forces at Dieppe with the number of Canadian prisoners lost during the last war will show that practically the same number of Canadian prisoners were taken from 1914 to 1918 as were lost in eight or nine hours at Dieppe.
The actual number of casualties at Dieppe works out, I believe, at sixty-seven per cent of all the troops that were engaged, and this includes the troops on various ships who did not disembark. The percentage of casualties among all those who did disembark is, I believe, well over seventy per cent.
The minister made certain references to reinforcements which are now overseas and are available to reinforce the army overseas.
But will he assure this committee that if the Canadian army is engaged in future operations of the same nature as the Dieppe operation, where the same percentage of casualties will apply, whether there are sufficient reinforcements to keep the two Canadian corps in England up to strength and to enable them to carry on as fighting units?
The chief of staff, General Stuart, has made certain remarks about the Dieppe affair which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of August 22.
My hon. friend said something about the two corps being engaged in similar operations to Dieppe. Does he mean that the two corps are a landing force?
I said future operations.
The whole two corps will be a landing force?
If they are all engaged. We do not know.
My hon. friend used the word "spearhead". He is mixing up bridgehead and spearhead.
I know what a bridgehead is and what a spearhead is.

I understood that a spearhead was used after the landing force had landed and made what they call a spearhead, that it was a force other than the landing force, and that the spearhead was landed afterwards to push on.
The minister knows that the Canadian corps has often been referred to as a dagger pointing at the heart of Berlin and that the Canadian forces would be the spearhead of the invasion.

Was my hon. friend
visualizing the two Canadian corps in a landing operation similar to Dieppe?
It will be like Dieppe, only on a much larger scale.
And he was visualizing that because the two Canadian corps, he said, were to be the spearhead. Isn't that what gave him that idea?
They will be part of the spearhead.

My understanding of a spearhead-probably I am wrong and my hon. friend is right-is that the spearhead would be something which landed and pushed on after the bridgehead had first been formed by other troops. The spearhead would press on.

Perhaps the minister is right. He is Minister of National Defence and would know more about it than I would.
War Appropriation-Army
My hon. friend said that he knew what a bridgehead was, and I thought he was mixing up bridgehead and spearhead.

General Stuart, chief of staff, is reported in the Vancouver Sun of August 22, 1942, as follows, describing the Dieppe operation:
Our soldiers walked into the hun's parlor through the front door at their own chosen time and left by the same front door when they wanted to leave.
I suggest that the actual facts are slightly different from the picture which General Stuart attempted to paint. This is the same officer who was chief of staff at the time of the Hong Kong disaster.
The minister himself has made reference outside the house to the Dieppe affair and is quoted by the Vancouver Sun as follows:
Dieppe was a thrust and a menace to the hun, and I believe it had something to do with the situation as it has since developed in North Africa and in Russia.
If Dieppe was the brilliant success which General Stuart and the minister state it was, perhaps the minister would be good enough to answer the question asked by the hon. member for Weyburn as to why General Roberts, one of the senior officers overseas, was taken out of a combatant position and placed in charge of reinforcements, which after all is purely an administrative post.

Far from it,
Mr. WHITE,:	Further, if Dieppe was the
brilliant success which it has been claimed to be by our chief of staff, why has Dieppe not been followed by operations of a similar kind by other Canadian or British or United States troops? If it has not been repeated by other similar operations, is it not because the cost in killed, wounded and prisoners of war, together with the loss of weapons, ammunition, equipment, ships, barges, and the loss in morale, make such operations prohibitive?

At the opening of
the session this winter I was one of those who asked the government to assure this nation that our army as now organized would be properly reinforced should they go into battle. Having followed very attentively the statement of the Minister of National Defence, I am not yet satisfied that this can be done if our army goes into battle as now organized and as an army. I am, on the contrary, of the opinion that this army has been overexpanded and overorganized-probably, as my

colleague from Vancouver South said, for political purposes rather than as an active army for operations.
Shame.

He was speaking of
man-power; and after all, they are both closely associated. I listened while the minister emphasized the fact that he had made it plain to Mr. Churchill, to Sir James Grigg, and to Sir Alan Brooke, the chief of the imperial general staff, that our army was available for service anywhere, either in whole or in part. He went on to explain that the army could be separated for service purposes. He rather left the impression, with me at least, that they were under the direction of British officials as to where they should serve, and in what manner. However, I have heard the minister state before that this government was entirely responsible for their operations; and on May 13, speaking of the Dieppe operation, as reported in Hansard, at page 2670, he also stated:
Reference was made to Canada to the war committee, which took the responsibility for authorizing Canadian participation.
That is, in that operation.
As to the matter of the Dieppe raid, I have been of opinion that we are not in a position to debate that operation properly. True enough, there is much information we cannot have until the war is over. I am of opinion that this operation probably resulted in the nazis obtaining more useful information, by the capture of operational orders and the many prisoners they took, than our authorities obtained. I believe that when the story can be fully told it will be shown that the nazis benefited from the operation more than we did.
In speaking on this matter I should like to associate myself with the remarks of my colleague the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough concerning the action of Padre Captain Jack Foote, who came originally from his constituency. I trust that the padre will receive proper recognition of his splendid work and of the gallant action he then took, followed up with work among his men in the prison camps, as conveyed in the message of which my colleague spoke.
This afternoon, when the minister was discussing man-power, I believe he stated that the need for men in industry had reached its peak and that there would now be many men available for other purposes in this country. If that is the situation, consider the statement

War Appropriation-Army
which was made by his colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, as reported in Hansard, at page 2622:
... I would point out that there is a very serious over-all shortage of man-power in war industry to-day. I know of very few plants that have the number of men required to permit them to obtain the desired output. What will happen will be a transfer of labour from plants making less urgently required equipment to plants making equipment for which there is greater urgency.
I suppose that will be carried through with other departments of government. It is proof to this committee and to the country that today there is still a lack of proper coordination between departments of government in the allocation of man-power. One has only to refer to the two statements of the two ministers most concerned in Canada to-day as regards man-power and the absolute contradiction expressed by those two ministers.
The minister went on to point out that there had been a number of postponements of cases of young men called from the agricultural sections of this country. I agree with him that there have been many postponements, but I do not agree with him in the policy which is still enunciated by this government. I am sure from his experience he knows as well as T do that many of these young men, when they receive their call to-day, despite the fact that they may realize they can render greater service on the farm, do not feel like asking for postponement; and it is simply a coercive method of forcing these chaps into the armed forces, because, when they receive their call, they have many pals overseas, and no matter where they may render the most useful service, they do not hesitate in many cases to enlist.
I have heard the minister say that national selective service would not benefit the air force. I think it is proven to-day that many of those young men who received the call but afterwards volunteered for service, when they were called, have rendered outstanding service in the air force. It was as a result first of all of conscription within Canada that many of those young men joined the armed forces, and yet they have proven to be the most outstanding chaps in the air force to-day.
There is one matter about which I am much concerned. I have addressed questions about it to the minister in the past; it is the medical branch of the army. He made some references this evening in rather slighting terms to the Globe and Mail. I wish to refer to a couple of articles which appeared in a newspaper which he will certainly regard in a different light from the Globe and Mail; that is, the Winnipeg Free Press, which through stormy weather or
fair believes that no wrong can be done by the present Prime Minister or his government. The Free Press of January 8 contains an article headed:
Suggestion to Mr. Ralston
It proceeds:
In these days when the shortage of doctors and nurses has become a matter of increasing danger to the civilian population of Canada, the Minister of Defence might usefully make inquiries into the extent of the training and activity undergone by No. 3 casualty clearing station which, mobilized in March, has been in these parts ever since.
That would be a year ago in March.
During that time it has made virtually no contribution to the war, and it has of course made none to the home front. The unit contains a large number of doctors and nurses, all of whom gave up useful practice in their sorely-needed and shorthanded professions for their country's sake. Since then they have been marking time.
Civilians are often properly told not to try. to probe into military secrets, but since it is the civilians who are paying the bills, their servant, the Minister of Defence, might well make the inquiry on their behalf and thereby allay the widespread feeling that there is both incompetence and inefficiency in a system which withdraws men and women from civilian life, gives them no useful training, and debars them for many months from making the very useful contribution they were formerly making to the life of the country.
That appeared, as I stated, on January 8, 1943. The same newspaper published the other day-I am not quite positive of the date-another editorial entitled:
Tlie Waste Continues
They state:
Last January on this page the Free Press addressed a short note to Mr. Ralston . . .
They go on to deal with the same subject, and ask him for an answer. I suppose he knows something about this, and I trust he will make an explanation to this committee regarding these questions which have been put to him, in a very pertinent manner, by a newspaper which is the staunchest supporter of the government of any journal in Canada. I will not read this article, because it is lengthy, but it is much to the point as far as the minister and his department are concerned.
Another article, of which I will read only a few lines, appeared in the Montreal Gazette of March 19. It begins:
Heavy drains upon the personnel of the medical and nursing profession here and in the United States are causing concern. They are the consequence of a commendably high sense of duty on the part of physicians and qualified nurses who believe their services should be given to the fighting forces. Their attitude is entirely praise-worthy. It is the resultant
War Appropriation-Army

difficulty which the civilian population is under in attempting to secure medical and nursing attendants that is giving rise to some anxiety.
It is part of the general manpower problem but it has its own exceptional features and these are of such importance from the general standpoint of public health as to call for immediate consideration. "Can we afford to waste medical skill when it is so limited?"
I trust the minister will have a proper explanation to give with reference to these matters. I am rather directly concerned at this time, because officials of the municipality of Roblin inform me that there is an area in southern Manitoba from Killarney east to Crystal city and north for a considerable distance from the United States border, covering an area of probably 2,000 square miles, without a medical practitioner, and the doctors at Killarney and Crystal city are old men. They cannot travel with the facility that they used to and there is a distinct lack of cooperation between the armed forces and the civilian population of the country.
With regard to this question of health, I should like to ask the minister a question as to just what the medical examination of a candidate is when he offers his services for enlistment.
The ordinary recruit?
Yes, any recruit.

The hon. member means
the medical examination of the recruit?

Yes, especially with regard to venereal disease. I believe a report was brought down this session, if I remember rightly, which indicated that he did not receive a proper examination at this stage, and the reason given was that it might hinder enlistment. I hope that is not regarded as a proper answer.
Was that a return?
I am not positive about that, but at any rate I trust the minister will make a statement in that regard.
I do not think that reason was given.
Can the minister say whether the men are examined for this disease at the time of enlistment?
I do not think they are, but immediately after.

I understand that they are not examined for it until they are sent to hospital for some condition. In my opinion this is very bad, and I say this because from my own province recent returns in the depart-

ment of health indicate that this disease is spreading, more particularly among the younger people, the teen-age people. It is assuming alarming proportions, and I certainly do not think our armed services are rendering the service to the nation which they should be when the authorities neglect to make this proper examination at the time men are taken in as recruits. I hope the minister will see his way to have a proper examination conducted, if it has not been the practice, because this disease, as a result of carelessness, might spread among the civilian population. This, I submit, is something to which the department should give serious consideration.
May I refer also to the question which the hon. member for Vancouver South brought up with reference to insurance of members of the armed forces, provided they are on active service, whether in Canada or overseas. He pointed out that there was no discrimination until May 21, 1940-I am not certain of the date-when by order in council the provision was rescinded so far as those serving in Canada were concerned. I could cite many examples from my owm community of men who offered themselves for active service, and the other day the minister, referring to a question on the order paper, stated that when a man offered his services he received orders as to where he should serve and should not be embarrassed by questions as to whether he was serving at headquarters or anywhere else. If that is so, the same principle should apply when a man offers his services for active service anywhere. Provision should be made that he be brought under the insurance principle that obtains overseas if he has offered himself for active service anywhere and serves in Canada, and I trust the department will see their way clear to bring all these men under the insurance principle.
There is another matter that has been bothering me for some time. In Great Britain, Prime Minister Churchill is recognized as commander-in-chief, and his word is law in any operation so far as the British empire is concerned. I believe the same applies in the United States; the President is commander-inchief. I do not think we have any recognized person in Canada in that capacity to-day. I do not believe that anyone is recognized here as commander-in-chief, and I submit that at this stage if we are to play our part as a nation-and we hear a great deal about our independence and our national status in this war-this question should receive attention, and someone in this government should be recognized as commander-in-chief, not only in military operations but as regards any

Public Accounts
difficulties such as we have had in the past in connection with man-power. If someone had had the backbone and the authority to issue orders as commander-in-chief, many things with respect to man-power might have been different from those that actually occurred. This is certainly something that should receive the attention of the Department of National Defence. Either the Prime Minister or someone else should be recognized as the proper authority in the capacity of commander-inchief throughout the duration of the war, with respect to man-power in and out of Canada, especially as regards those Canadians who are connected with the war effort. Mr. Speaker, may I call it eleven o'clock?
Progress reported.
